definition: In perfect condition or order.
In perfect condition or order.
(of quantities) imprecise but fairly close to correct.
example: In just about a minute.
etymology: Adjective from Middle English about (adverb).

definition: (in writing) at an earlier place.
example: He’s in a better place now, floating free as the clouds above.
etymology: The preposition, the adjective, and the noun derive from the adverb.

definition: The right to enter.
example: The door provides access to the premises.
etymology: From Middle English accesse, acces, borrowed from Middle French acces (“attack, onslaught”) or from its source Latin accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach;

definition: A record or narrative description of past events.
example: He gave an inaccurate account of the plot to kill the president.
etymology: From Old French acounter, accomptere et al., from a- + conter (“to count”)). Compare count.

definition: To the opposite side.
example: The football field was 300 feet across.
etymology: From Middle English acros, from early Middle English a-croiz, a-creoyz, from Anglo-Norman an (“in, on”) + croiz (“in the form of a cross”). More at cross. By surface analysis, a- + cross.

definition: Perform an action, or work out or perform (an action).
example: Think before you act.
etymology: From Middle English acte, from Old French acte, from Latin ācta (“register of events”), plural of āctum (“decree, law”), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti.

definition: Something done (usually as opposed to something said).
example: There were stories of murders and other unnatural actions.

definition: In actual fact.
example: To be nominally but not actually independent.
etymology: From Middle English actually, actuelly, equivalent to actual + -ly.

definition: A software module that extends or enhances the capabilities of an existing application.
etymology: Deverbal from add on.

definition: A component that is added to something to improve it.
example: The addition of a bathroom was a major improvement.
etymology: Sense of “what is added” dates from 14th century, from Middle English addicioun, addition, from Old French adition, from Latin additiōnem, accusative singular of additiō, from addō (“add, put”).

definition: Happening at a time subsequent to a reference time.
example: It didn't happen until afterward.
etymology: The Irish usage to indicate recent completion of an activity is a calque of the Irish collocation Táim tar éis... (“I have just...”, literally “I am after...”).

definition: Anew.
example: She tried again.
etymology: From Middle English agayn, from Old English onġēan (“against, again”), from Proto-West Germanic *in gagin, from Proto-Germanic *in gagin.

definition: How long something has existed.
example: It was replaced because of its age.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English agen, from the noun. Originally found mostly as a participial adjective, probably an adjective in -ed, derived from the noun, reanalyzed to create a verb;

definition: Belonging to or lasting from times long ago.
example: Age-old customs.

definition: Gone by; or in the past.
example: Two years ago.

definition: At or in the front.
example: I see the lights of a town ahead.
etymology: From a- + head. Perhaps originally a nautical term, beyond the head (of a ship), then drifting into more general English usage where it is used to describe something as being in front of.

definition: Using all available resources.
example: All-out war.
etymology: From all + out.

definition: Unsurpassed in some respect up to the present.
example: Prices at an all-time high.
etymology: From all + time.

definition: Make it possible through a specific action or lack of action for something to happen.
example: This sealed door won't allow the water to come into the basement.
etymology: The similarity with Middle English alyfen (from Old English ālīefan) and German erlauben, both from Proto-Germanic *uzlaubijaną (“to allow”), is coincidental.

definition: (of actions or states) slightly short of or not quite accomplished; all but.
example: The baby was almost asleep when the alarm sounded.
etymology: From Middle English almost, from Old English eallmǣst (“nearly all, almost, for the most part”), equivalent to al- (“all”) + most.

definition: Isolated from others.
example: Could be alone in a crowded room.
etymology: From Middle English allone, from earlier all oon (literally “all one”), contracted from the Old English phrase eall ān (“completely alone”), equivalent to al- (“all”) + one.

definition: With a forward motion.
example: We drove along admiring the view.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old English andlang, from prefix and- + lang (“long”). Doublet of endlong.

definition: Prior to a specified or implied time.
example: She has already graduated.

definition: In addition.
example: Everyone had eggs for breakfast, but Alice also had toast. Also, she finished hers in under half an hour.
etymology: From Middle English also, alswo, alswa (also als(e), as, whence English as), from Old English eallswā (“just like, also”), from Proto-West Germanic *allswā, equivalent to all + so.

definition: At all times; all the time and on every occasion.
example: I will always be there to help you.

definition: Surprising greatly.
example: She does an amazing amount of work.
etymology: From amaze + -ing, from Old English āmasian.

definition: A quantity of money.
example: The amount he had in cash was insufficient.

definition: React verbally.
example: She didn't want to answer.

definition: In the area or vicinity.
example: Hanging around.
etymology: From Middle English around, arounde, from a- (from Old English a- (“on, at”)) + Middle English round (“circle, round”) borrowed from French, equivalent to a- + round. Cognate with Scots aroond, aroon (“around”).

definition: The products of human creativity; works of art collectively.
example: An art exhibition.
etymology: From Middle English art, from Old French art, from Latin artem, accusative of ars (“art”). Partly displaced native Old English cræft, whence Modern English craft.

definition: Make a request or demand for something to somebody.
example: She asked him for a loan.
etymology: From Middle English asken, axen, from Old English āscian, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish; request”).

definition: Of or befitting a lord.
example: Of august lineage.
etymology: From French auguste (“noble, stately; august”) or Latin augustus (“majestic, venerable, august; imperial, royal”), from augeō (“to augment, increase; to enlarge, expand, spread”). Doublet of August and Augustus.

definition: From a particular thing or place or position (‘forth’ is obsolete).
example: Ran away from the lion.
etymology: From Middle English away, awey, awei, oway, o wey, on way, from Old English āweġ, onweġ (“away”), originally on weġ (“on one's way; onward; on”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + way.

definition: A very young child (birth to 1 year) who has not yet begun to walk or talk.
example: The baby began to cry again.
etymology: From Middle English baby, babie (“baby”), a diminutive form of babe (“babe, baby”), equivalent to babe + -y/-ie (“endearing and diminutive suffix”). Perhaps ultimately imitative of baby talk (compare babble).

definition: Be behind; approve of.
example: I backed Kennedy in 1960.
etymology: Compare Middle Low German bak (“back”), from Old Saxon bak, and West Frisian bekling (“chair back”), Old High German bah, Swedish and Norwegian bak. Cognate with German Bache (“sow [adult female hog]”).

definition: Having undesirable or negative qualities.
example: A bad report card.
etymology: From Middle English bad, badde (“wicked, evil, depraved”), of uncertain origin.

definition: Sloping land (especially the slope beside a body of water).
example: They pulled the canoe up on the bank.
etymology: For the bench-bank relation, compare typologically Russian ла́вка (lávka), прила́вок (prilávok).

definition: Installation from which a military force initiates operations.
example: The attack wiped out our forward bases.
etymology: From Middle English base, bas, baas, from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). Doublet of basis and bass.

definition: Having a base.
example: Firmly based ice.
etymology: From base + -ed.

definition: Enter or assume a certain state or condition.
example: The weather will become cold after the sun goes down.
etymology: A compound of the sources of be- + come. From Middle English becomen, bicumen, from Old English becuman (“to come (to), approach, arrive, enter, meet with, fall in with; happen, befall;

definition: A piece of furniture that provides a place to sleep.
example: He sat on the edge of the bed.
etymology: The Proto-Germanic term may in turn be from Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰ- (“to dig”) with various theories explaining the development in meaning.

definition: Earlier in time; previously.
example: I had known her before.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”).

definition: In or to or toward the rear.
example: He followed behind.

definition: The state or fact of existing.
example: A point of view gradually coming into being.
etymology: Originated 1250–1300 from Middle English being; see be + -ing.

definition: Accept as true; take to be true.
example: I believed his report.
etymology: The prepositionally transitive senses with in are a semantic loan from Latin crēdō in aliquem / aliquid.

definition: In or to a place that is lower.
example: The town is situated on a hillside, with a river running below.
etymology: From Middle English bilooghe, equivalent to be- + low. Compare also earlier Middle English alogh, alow, aloȝ, alowe (“below”), benethen (“beneath”), Dutch omlaag (“downwards”).

definition: In a most excellent way or manner.
example: He played best after a couple of martinis.
etymology: From Middle English best, beste, from Old English bezt, betest, from Proto-Germanic *batistaz.

definition: In the interval.
example: Dancing all the dances with little rest between.

definition: A statute in draft before it becomes law.
example: They held a public hearing on the bill.
etymology: From Middle English bille, from Anglo-Norman bille, from Old French bulle, from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal, sealed document”). Doublet of bull (“papal bull; bubble”) and bulla.

definition: A small piece or quantity of something.
example: A bit of paper.
etymology: From Middle English bitte, bite, from Old English bita (“bit; fragment; morsel”) and bite (“a bite; cut”), from Proto-Germanic *bitô and *bitiz; both from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”). More at bite.

definition: A committee having supervisory powers.
example: The board has seven members.
etymology: Board (duplicate bridge) From Middle English boord, boorde, bord, bourd, burd, from Old English bord, from Proto-West Germanic *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, plank; edge;

definition: A written work or composition that has been published (printed on pages bound together).
example: I am reading a good book on economics.
etymology: From Middle English booken, boken, from Old English bōcian, ġebōcian, from the noun (see above).

definition: Brought into existence.
example: He was a child born of adultery.
etymology: Dialectal variant of burn.

definition: (used with count nouns) two considered together; the two.
example: Both girls are pretty.
etymology: From Middle English bothe, boþe, from Old English bā þā (“both the; both those”) and possibly reinforced by Old Norse báðir, from Proto-Germanic *bai.

definition: A (usually rectangular) container; may have a lid.
example: He rummaged through a box of spare parts.
etymology: (motor racing): Used since it is more distinct over the radio compared to pit. Also from German Boxenstopp (“pit stop”).

definition: A youthful male person.
example: The baby was a boy.
etymology: Cognate with Scots boy (“boy”), West Frisian boai (“boy”), Dutch boi (“boy”), Low German Boi (“boy”), and probably to the Old English proper name Bōia.

definition: Terminate or end.
example: Break a lucky streak.
etymology: The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English /ɛː/ to /eɪ/ in the standard language; contrast this with the development of other words such as speak and wreak.

definition: Trespassing for an unlawful purpose; illegal entrance into premises with criminal intent.
example: There was a break-in at the shop; everything was taken.
etymology: Deverbal from break in.

definition: Take something or somebody with oneself somewhere.
example: Bring me the box from the other room.
etymology: Onomatopoeia.

definition: A male with the same parents as someone else.
example: My brother still lives with our parents.

definition: Make by combining materials and parts.
example: He will build an organization equipped for success.

definition: A structure that has a roof and walls and stands more or less permanently in one place.
example: There was a three-story building on the corner.
etymology: From Middle English bildynge, byldynge, equivalent to build + -ing. Compare also related Middle English bold (“edifice, castle, mansion”), from Old English bold (“building, dwelling, house”).

definition: Existing as an essential constituent or characteristic.
example: The Ptolemaic system with its built-in concept of periodicity.

definition: Peopled with settlers.
example: The built-up areas.

definition: A commercial or industrial enterprise and the people who constitute it.
example: He bought his brother's business.
etymology: From Middle English busines, busynes, businesse, bisynes, from Old English bisiġnes (“business, busyness”), equivalent to busy + -ness. Doublet of busyness.

definition: And nothing more.
example: Hopes that last but a moment.
etymology: From Middle English but, buten, boute, bouten, from Old English būtan (“without, outside of, except, only”), from Proto-West Germanic *biūtan, *biūtini, equivalent to be- + out.

definition: Obtain by purchase; acquire by means of a financial transaction.
example: She buys for the big department store.
etymology: Cognate with Scots buy (“to buy, purchase”), obsolete Dutch beugen (“to buy”), Old Saxon buggian, buggean (“to buy”), Old Norse byggja (“to build, settle”), Gothic 𐌱𐌿𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bugjan, “to buy”).

definition: A line giving the name of the writer of a story or article.
Assign a specified (usually proper) name to.
A challenge to a fight or duel.
etymology: Deverbal from call out.

definition: A race between candidates for elective office.
example: I managed his campaign for governor.
etymology: From French campagne, from Italian campagna (“field, military operation”), from Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of campania, campagna, and champagne.

definition: Marked by a willingness to tackle a job and get it done.
example: A can-do kind of person.
etymology: From can + do.

definition: Assets available for use in the production of further assets.
example: He does not have enough capital to start a business.
etymology: From Middle English capital, borrowed partly from Old French capital and partly from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (in sense “head of cattle”), from caput (“head”) (English cap) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives).

definition: The work of providing treatment for or attending to someone or something.
example: No medical care was required.
etymology: From Middle English caren, carien, from Old English carian (“to sorrow, grieve, be troubled, be anxious, to care for, heed”), from Proto-West Germanic *karōn (“to care”), from Proto-Germanic *karōną (“to care”).

definition: The particular occupation for which you are trained.
example: Washington’s career as a soldier.
etymology: Mid 16th century, from French carrière (“road;

definition: An occurrence of something.
example: It was a case of bad judgment.
etymology: From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).

definition: Events that provide the generative force that is the origin of something.
example: They are trying to determine the cause of the crash.

definition: An area that is approximately central within some larger region.
example: It is in the center of town.
etymology: * (group theory): In the notation Z(G), the letter Z derives from the German Zentrum (“center”).

definition: Serving as an essential component.
example: The central cause of the problem.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin centrālis, from centrum (“centre”), from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron); by surface analysis, centre + -al.

definition: Definite but not specified or identified.
example: Set aside a certain sum each week.

definition: A possibility due to a favorable combination of circumstances.
example: Now is your chance.
etymology: From Middle English chance, cheance, chaunce, cheaunce, a borrowing from Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”), from Latin cadere (“to fall, to die, to happen, occur”).

definition: An event that occurs when something passes from one state or phase to another.
example: The change was intended to increase sales.

definition: Made or become different in nature or form.
example: Changed attitudes.

definition: Examine so as to determine accuracy, quality, or condition.
example: Check the brakes.
etymology: All of the English senses developed from the chess sense.

definition: The act of reporting your presence (as at an airport or a hotel).
A person who is in charge.
etymology: Doublet of cape (“point of land”), capo, caput, and chef through Latin (possibly also related to cape (“sleeveless garment”) and cap (“head covering”) from Latin cappa);

definition: High quality porcelain originally made only in China.
example: It's a china doll.
etymology: From clippings of attributive use of China, q.v., the country in East Asia.

definition: The person or thing chosen or selected.
example: Do I have a choice of what color to paint it?
etymology: From Middle English choys, from a merger of the noun above and Middle English chyse, chuse, chys, chis (“choice, excellent”), from Old English ċīes (“choice; dainty; nice”), related to Old English ċēosan (“to choose”).

definition: One of the groups of Christians who have their own beliefs and forms of worship.
A collection of things sharing a common attribute.
example: There are two classes of detergents.

definition: Rid of obstructions.
example: Clear your desk.
etymology: From Middle English clere, from Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler (Modern French clair), from Latin clarus.

definition: Move so that an opening or passage is obstructed; make shut.
example: Close the door.
etymology: From Middle English closen (“to close, enclose”), partly continuing (in altered form) earlier Middle English clusen (“to close”) from Old English clȳsan (“to close, shut”);

definition: A team of professional baseball players who play and travel together.
example: Each club played six home games with teams in its own division.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English clubbe, from Old Norse klubba, klumba (“cudgel”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“clip, clasp; clump, lump; log, block”). Doublets of English clump, cloud, Latin globus, glomus;

definition: The body of faculty and students of a college.
etymology: From Middle English college, from Middle French college, from Old French college, from Latin collēgium. Doublet of collegium.

definition: Anything that serves as an enticement.
example: The free offers are just come-ons to get you in the store so the sales staff can work on you.
etymology: Deverbal from come on to. First use appears c. 1897, in the publications of Edward W. Townsend. See cite below.

definition: The act of drawing spatially closer to something.
example: The coming of a season.
etymology: From Middle English cominge, comynge, comande, from Old English cumende, from Proto-Germanic *kwemandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), equivalent to come + -ing (present participle ending).

definition: Belonging to or participated in by a community as a whole; public.
example: For the common good.

definition: An institution created to conduct business.
example: He only invests in large well-established companies.
etymology: From Middle English companye (“a team; companionship”), from Old French compaignie (“companionship”) (Modern French: compagnie), possibly from Late Latin *compania, but this word is not attested.

definition: Having every necessary or normal part or component or step.
example: A complete meal.

definition: Continue a certain state, condition, or activity.
example: We continued to work into the night.
etymology: From Middle English continuen, from Old French continuer, from Latin continuō. Displaced native Middle English thurghwonen, from Old English þurhwunian.

definition: The total spent for goods or services including money and time and labor.
example: The total cost of the new complex was an estimated $1.5 million.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English costen (verb), borrowed from Old French coster, from Medieval Latin cōstō, from Latin cōnstō, from Proto-Italic *komstaēō. By surface analysis, con- (“together”) + stō (“stand”).

definition: A body serving in an administrative capacity.
example: Student council.

definition: A politically organized body of people under a single government.
example: The country's largest manufacturer.
etymology: Compare typologically Russian страна́ (straná), сторона́ (storoná).

definition: A pair who associate with one another.
example: The engaged couple.
etymology: From Middle English couple, from Old French couple, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula.

definition: Education imparted in a series of lessons or meetings.
example: He took a course in basket weaving.
etymology: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of cursus and cour.

definition: Provide with a covering or cause to be covered.
example: Cover her face with a handkerchief.
etymology: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the original sense of the verb and noun cover was “hide from view” as in its cognate covert.

definition: Concealment that attempts to prevent something scandalous from becoming public.
etymology: Deverbal from cover up.

definition: Affected with madness or insanity.
example: His ideas were both frightening and crazy.
etymology: From craze (“to crush”) + -y, akin to being "crazed up". Compare cracked up (“suffered a mental breakdown; be insane”), crackpot. Compare typologically Russian чо́кнутый (čóknutyj).

definition: Make or cause to be or to become.
example: Create a furor.
etymology: From Middle English createn, from Latin creātus, the perfect passive participle of creō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Approval.
example: He was given credit for his work.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French crédit (“belief, trust”), from Latin crēditum (“a loan, credit”), neuter of crēditus, past participle of crēdere (“to believe”). The verb is from the noun. Doublet of shraddha, creed.

definition: Travel across or pass over.
example: She frowned and crossed her arms.
etymology: *Saterland Frisian Krjuus, Kjus (“cross”)

definition: A particular society at a particular time and place.
etymology: From Middle French culture (“cultivation; culture”), from Latin cultūra (“cultivation;

definition: Separate with or as if with an instrument.
example: Cut the rope.

definition: (broadcasting) a local announcement inserted into a network program.
etymology: Deverbal from cut in.

definition: Someone who plays practical jokes on others.
etymology: Deverbal from cut up.

definition: Of or belonging to or occurring every day.
example: Daily routine.
etymology: From Middle English dayly, from Old English dæġlīċ, from Proto-West Germanic *dagalīk, from Proto-Germanic *dagalīkaz (“daily”), equivalent to day + -ly.

definition: Devoid of or deficient in light or brightness; shadowed or black.
example: Sitting in a dark corner.
etymology: From Middle English derk, derke, dirke, dyrke, from the adjective (see above), or possibly from an unrecorded Old English *dierce, *diercu (“dark, darkness”).

definition: The specified day of the month.
example: What is the date today?
etymology: From Middle English date, from Old French date, from Late Latin data, from Latin datus (“given”), past participle of dare (“to give”); from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”). Doublet of data.

definition: Time for Earth to make a complete rotation on its axis.
example: Two days later they left.

definition: Not fresh today.
example: Day-old bread is cheaper than fresh.

definition: The time during which someone's life continues.
example: The monarch's last days.
etymology: From Middle English dayes, dawes, from Old English dagas, from Proto-Germanic *dagōs, *dagōz, plural of *dagaz, equivalent to day + -s (plural ending).

definition: No longer having or seeming to have or expecting to have life.
example: The nerve is dead.
etymology: From Middle English ded, deed, from Old English dēad, from Proto-West Germanic *daud, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz.

definition: Lacking opportunities for development or advancement.
example: Stuck in a dead-end job.

definition: Accurate and to the point.
example: A dead-on feel for characterization.

definition: Act on verbally or in some form of artistic expression.
example: This book deals with incest.
etymology: From Middle English del, dele, from Old English dǣl (“part, share, portion”), from Proto-West Germanic *daili, from Proto-Germanic *dailiz (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo- (“part, watershed”).

definition: Recognizable; marked.
example: At a distinct (or decided) disadvantage.

definition: The act of making up your mind about something.
example: The burden of decision was his.
etymology: Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

definition: Relatively deep or strong; affecting one deeply.
example: A deep breath.

definition: The act of working out the form of something (as by making a sketch or outline or plan).
example: He contributed to the design of a new instrument.
etymology: From Middle English designen, from Old French designer, from Latin designō (“to mark out, point out, describe, design, contrive”), from de- (or dis-) + signō (“to mark”), from signum (“mark”). Doublet of designate.

definition: Lack of respect accompanied by a feeling of intense dislike.
example: The despite in which outsiders were held is legendary.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English despit, dispit, from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”).

definition: Someone who controls resources and expenditures.
A region marked off for administrative or other purposes.
Having finished or arrived at completion.
example: Certain to make history before he's done.
etymology: From Middle English don, idon, ydon, ȝedon, gedon, from Old English dōn, ġedōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dān, from Proto-Germanic *dēnaz (past participle of *dōną (“to do”)).

definition: Being or moving lower in position or less in some value.
example: Lay face down.
etymology: Cognate with West Frisian dún (“dune, sandhill”), Dutch duin (“dune, sandhill”), German Düne (“dune”). More at town; akin to dune. Doublet of Down.

definition: Operate or control a vehicle.
example: Drive a car or bus.
etymology: From Middle English dryven, from Old English drīfan (“to drive, force, move”), from Proto-West Germanic *drīban, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”).

definition: Any installation designed to accommodate patrons in their automobiles.
etymology: Deverbal from drive in.

definition: Owed and payable immediately or on demand.
example: Payment is due.
etymology: From Middle English dewe, dew, due, from Old French deü (“due”), past participle of devoir (“to owe”), from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”), from dē- (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).

definition: The cardinal compass point that is at 90 degrees.
example: Portsmouth is to the east of Southampton.

definition: Take in solid food.
example: She was eating a banana.
etymology: From Middle English eten, from Old English etan (“to eat”), from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną (“to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti, from *h₁ed- (“to eat”).

definition: Of or relating to an economy, the system of production and management of material wealth.
example: Economic growth.
etymology: The adjective is derived from the noun; compare the adjective senses in Middle and Old French, Latin, and Ancient Greek.

definition: A phenomenon that follows and is caused by some previous phenomenon.
example: The magnetic effect was greater when the rod was lengthwise.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of seven and one.
A vote to select the winner of a position or political office.
example: The results of the election will be announced tonight.
etymology: From Middle English eleccioun, eleccion, from Anglo-Norman eleccioun, from Latin ēlectiōn-, stem of ēlectiō (“choice, selection”), from ēligō (“to pluck out, to choose”). Equivalent to elect + -ion.

definition: Either extremity of something that has length.
example: The end of the pier.
etymology: From Middle English ende, from Old English ende, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos (“forehead; front”), from *h₂ent- (“face; forehead;

definition: The ultimate goal.
example: Human beings are not the end-all of evolution.

definition: Derive or receive pleasure from; get enjoyment from; take pleasure in.
example: Enjoy your holidays! I very much enjoy dancing.
etymology: From Middle English enjoyen, from Old French enjoier, anjoier, enjoer (“to give joy, receive with joy, rejoice”), equivalent to en- + joy.

definition: Sufficient for the purpose.
example: Enough food.

definition: Constituting the full quantity or extent; complete.
example: An entire town devastated by an earthquake.
etymology: From Middle English entere, enter, borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (“whole”). Doublet of entier and integer.

definition: Divisible by two.
example: Clear out those rocks. The surface must be even.
etymology: From Middle English even, from Old English efn (“flat; level, even, equal”), from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)em-no- (“equal, straight; flat, level, even”).

definition: Something that happens at a given place and time.
etymology: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”);

definition: At any time.
example: Did you ever smoke?

definition: Your basis for belief or disbelief; knowledge on which to base belief.
example: The evidence that smoking causes lung cancer is very compelling.
etymology: From Middle English evidence, from Old French [Term?], from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.

definition: Indicating exactness or preciseness.
example: He was doing precisely (or exactly) what she had told him to do.
etymology: From exact + -ly.

definition: An item of information that is typical of a class or group.
example: This patient provides a typical example of the syndrome.
etymology: From Middle English example, exaumple, from Old French example, essaumple, from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”, literally “what is taken out”); see exempt.

definition: Object to.
example: I find most people annoying — present company excepted, of course!
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

definition: Regard something as probable or likely.
example: The meteorologists are expecting rain for tomorrow.
etymology: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (“look out for, await, expect”), from ex (“out”) + spectō (“look at”), frequentative of speciō (“see”).

definition: Opinion or judgment.
example: In the eyes of the law.

definition: The front of the human head from the forehead to the chin and ear to ear.
example: He washed his face.
etymology: In the sense of face as in reputation, influenced by Chinese 面子 (miànzi) or 臉／脸 (liǎn), both of which mean literally the front of the head and metaphorically one's public image. See lose face.

definition: A hostile disagreement face-to-face.
example: It's unclear which side will win the latest face-off between the President and Congress.
etymology: From face + off, or a deverbal from face off, c. 1889.

definition: A piece of information about circumstances that exist or events that have occurred.
example: First you must collect all the facts of the case.
etymology: From Old French fact, from Latin factum (“an act, deed, feat, etc.”); also Medieval Latin for “state, condition, circumstance”;

definition: Descend in free fall under the influence of gravity.
example: To fall the voice.
etymology: Perhaps from the north-eastern Scottish pronunciation of whale.

definition: A social unit living together.
example: He moved his family to Virginia.
etymology: From Late Middle English famylye, from Latin familia (“a household”). Displaced native Old English hīred and hād. Doublet of familia.

definition: To a considerable degree; very much.
example: A far far better thing that I do.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English ferre, fer, Old English feor, feorr, from Proto-Germanic *ferrai.

definition: Very far away in space or time.
example: Troops landing on far-off shores.
etymology: Univerbation of far off (adverb).

definition: (informal) strikingly unconventional.
A male parent (also used as a term of address to your father).
example: His father was born in Atlanta.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fader, from Old English fæder, from Proto-West Germanic *fader, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr, possibly from *peh₂- + *-tḗr.

definition: Of or relating to the central government of a federation.
example: A federal district is one set aside as the seat of the national government.
etymology: Borrowed from French fédéral, from Latin foedus + French -al.

definition: Undergo an emotional sensation or be in a particular state of mind.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch voelen and German fühlen.

definition: The experiencing of affective and emotional states.
example: She had a feeling of euphoria.
etymology: From Middle English felynge, equivalent to feel + -ing.

definition: Mat together and make felt-like.
example: Felt the wool.
etymology: From Old English fēled, corresponding to feel + -ed.

definition: A hostile meeting of opposing military forces in the course of a war.
A diagram or picture illustrating textual material.
example: The area covered can be seen from Figure 2.

definition: Occurring at or forming an end or termination.
example: The final chapter.
etymology: From Middle English final, fynal, fynall, from Old French final, from Latin fīnālis (“of or relating to the end or to boundaries”), from fīnis (“end”); see fine. Replaced native English endly (“final”).

definition: After an unspecified period of time or an especially long delay.
example: The contest was long, but the Romans finally conquered.
etymology: From Middle English finally, fynaly, fynally, fynaliche, fynalliche, equivalent to final + -ly.

definition: Come upon, as if by accident; meet with.
example: We find this idea in Plato.
etymology: For the meaning development compare Proto-Slavic *najьti > Russian найти́ (najtí), akin to Proto-Slavic *jьti > идти́ (idtí); Russian находи́ть (naxodítʹ), нахо́дка (naxódka), akin to ход (xod), ходи́ть (xodítʹ).

definition: Being satisfactory or in satisfactory condition.
example: Everything's fine.
etymology: From Middle English fyn, fyne, from Old French fin, from Medieval Latin fīnis (“a payment in settlement or tax”). Doublet of fin and finis.

definition: The first or highest in an ordering or series.
example: He wanted to be the first.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of four and one.
example: He wrote a five followed by four zeroes.

definition: The concentration of attention or energy on something.
example: The focus of activity shifted to molecular biology.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”); see there for more. Related to fuel.

definition: To travel behind, go after, come after.
example: The ducklings followed their mother around the pond.
etymology: From Middle English folwen, folȝen, folgen, from Old English folgian (“to follow, pursue”), from Proto-West Germanic *folgēn, from Proto-Germanic *fulgāną (“to follow”).

definition: Any substance that can be metabolized by an animal to give energy and build tissue.
example: The innkeeper brought them food and drink.

definition: Of concern to or concerning the affairs of other nations (other than your own).
example: Foreign trade.
etymology: The silent -g- added perhaps by analogy with reign (compare also sovereign which was similarly altered).

definition: Dismiss from the mind; stop remembering.
example: Let's just forget I ever told you anything about it.
etymology: From Middle English forgeten, forgiten, foryeten, forȝiten, from Old English forġietan (“to forget”) [influenced by Old Norse geta ("to get, to guess")], from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan (“to give up, forget”).

definition: At or to or toward the front; forward.
example: He faced forward.
etymology: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“forward, inclined to the front, fore, early, former”), from Proto-Germanic *fura- (“fore-”), *warþaz (“turned”), equivalent to fore + -ward.

definition: Set up or found.
etymology: From Middle English founden, from Old French founder (Modern French: fonder), from Latin fundāre. Compare fund.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of three and one.
example: Do you have any more fours? I want to make this a little taller.

definition: Grant freedom to; free from confinement.
etymology: Germanic and Celtic are the only Indo-European language branches in which the PIE word with the meaning of "dear, beloved" acquired the additional meaning of "free" in the sense of "not in bondage".

definition: A person you know well and regard with affection and trust.
example: He was my best friend at the university.

definition: Containing as much or as many as is possible or normal.
example: A full glass.
etymology: From Middle English ful, from Old English full (“full”), from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

definition: Activities that are enjoyable or amusing.
example: I do it for the fun of it.

definition: Yet to be or coming.
example: Some future historian will evaluate him.
etymology: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”).

definition: Applying to all or most members of a category or group.
example: The general public.
etymology: From Middle English general, in turn from Anglo-Norman general, generall, Middle French general, and their source, Latin generālis, from genus (“class, kind”) + -ālis (“-al”).

definition: Come into the possession of something concrete or abstract.
example: Get your results the next day.
etymology: Cognate with Yola get (“to get”), Danish gide (“to care, like”), Faroese gita (“to be able”), Icelandic geta (“to be able; to beget, father; to achieve, obtain, to guess;

definition: The time at which something is supposed to begin.
example: She knew from the get-go that he was the man for her.
etymology: From get + go. First use appears in 1960 as part of the phrase from the get-go in the publication Baltimore Afro-American.

definition: The act of acquiring something.
example: He's much more interested in the getting than in the giving.

definition: A young female.
etymology: From Middle English gerle, girle, gyrle (“young person (boy or girl)”), perhaps from Old English *gyrele, from Proto-West Germanic *gurilā, from a zero-grade diminutive of *gaurā (“young child”) + *-ilā.

definition: Cause to have, in the abstract sense or physical sense.
Acknowledged as a supposition.
example: Given the engine's condition, it is a wonder that it started.
etymology: Morphologically give + -n.

definition: The act of giving.
etymology: By surface analysis, give + -ing.

definition: An action or object one always chooses first.
example: Going for a drink after work is usually my go-to.
etymology: A univerbation of go + to. Compare typologically convenient, Russian подходя́щий (podxodjáščij) (<~ ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).

definition: The act of departing.
example: The going was very difficult over the ice.

definition: Coins made of gold.
example: The pirates were searching for gold.
etymology: From gold master, a copy of the code certified as being ready for release.

definition: A farewell remark.
example: They said their good-byes.

definition: Relatively large in size or number or extent; larger than others of its kind.
example: A great juicy steak.
etymology: From Middle English greet, grete (“great, large”), from Old English grēat (“big, massive; tall; thick; coarse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz (“coarse, crude;

definition: The solid part of the earth's surface.
example: He dropped the logs on the ground.
etymology: (to punish): Compare (to bring) down to earth, to come down to earth.

definition: Any number of entities (members) considered as a unit.
etymology: Cognate with German Kropf (“crop, craw, bunch”); Old English cropp, croppa (“cluster, bunch, sprout, flower, berry, ear of corn, crop”) (whence English crop); Dutch krop (“craw”), Icelandic kroppr (“hump, bunch”).

definition: Expect, believe, or suppose.
example: I guess she is angry at me for standing her up.

definition: An informal term for a youth or man.
example: A nice guy.
etymology: Coined by semantic widening from the name of Guy Fawkes (1570–1606), an English Catholic executed for his role in the Gunpowder Plot, which also came to refer to effigies of his image burned annually on Guy Fawkes Night.

definition: Reduced wage paid to someone who is not working full time.
Involving active participation.
example: He's a hands-on manager.
etymology: Possibly from the phrase all hands on deck.

definition: Come to pass.
example: What is happening?

definition: Dislike intensely; feel antipathy or aversion towards.
example: I hate Mexican food.
etymology: From Middle English haate, hat, hate (noun), probably from Old English hatian (“to hate”, verb) and/or Old Norse hatr (“hate”, noun).

definition: Have or possess, either in a concrete or an abstract sense.
example: I have two years left.
etymology: From have on (“to deceive”).

definition: A person with few or no possessions.
Characterized by direct opposition.
example: A head-on confrontation.

definition: A healthy state of wellbeing free from disease.
example: Physicians should be held responsible for the health of their patients.
etymology: From Middle English heleð (“man, hero, fighter”), from Old English hæleþ (“man, hero, fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, from Proto-Germanic *haliþaz (“man, hero”).

definition: Perceive (sound) via the auditory sense.
Detected or perceived by the sense of hearing.
example: A conversation heard through the wall.

definition: Occupied or in the control of; often used in combination.
example: Enemy-held territory.

definition: Give help or assistance; be of service.
example: Everyone helped out during the earthquake.
etymology: From Middle English help, from Old English help (“help, aid, assistance, relief”), from Proto-Germanic *helpō (“help”), *hilpiz, *hulpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).

definition: In or at this place; where the speaker or writer is.
example: I work here.
etymology: From Middle English her, from Old English hēr (“at this place”), from Proto-West Germanic *hēr, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r, from *hiz + *-r, from Proto-Indo-European *kís, from *ḱe + *ís.

definition: Greater than normal in quantity or amount.
example: A high temperature.

definition: Poker in which the high and low hands split the pot.
(of shoes or boots) having relatively high uppers.
An important or influential (and often overbearing) person.
Advanced in complexity or elaboration.
example: Higher finance.

definition: The aggregate of past events.
example: A critical time in the school's history.
etymology: Attested in Middle English in 1393 by John Gower, Confessio Amantis, which was aimed at an educated audience familiar with French and Latin.

definition: Cause to continue in a certain state, position, or activity.
example: Hold in place.
etymology: Compare Latin celer (“quick”), Tocharian B käl- (“to goad, drive”), Ancient Greek κέλλω (kéllō, “to drive”), Sanskrit कलयति (kalayati, “to impel”).

definition: Where you live at a particular time.
example: Deliver the package to my home.

definition: Roll, press, forge, or shape (metal) while hot.
A period of time equal to 1/24th of a day.
example: The job will take more than an hour.

definition: A period of time assigned for work.
example: They work long hours.

definition: A dwelling that serves as living quarters for one or more families.
example: He has a house on Cape Cod.
etymology: From Middle English housen, from Old English hūsian, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną (“to house, live, dwell”), from the noun (see above).

definition: Despite anything to the contrary (usually preceding a concession).
example: Although I'm a little afraid, however I'd like to try it.
etymology: From Middle English however, how-ever, how-evere; equivalent to how + -ever. Compare howsoever.

definition: Unusually great in size or amount or degree or especially extent or scope.
example: Huge government spending.
etymology: From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of unknown origin.

definition: Characteristic of humanity.
example: Human nature.
etymology: From Late Middle English humaigne, humayne, humain, from Middle French humain, from Old French humain, umain (“of or belonging to man”, adjective), from Latin hūmānus m (“of man, human”, adjective);

definition: A married man; a woman's partner in marriage.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English husbonde, from Old English hūsbonda, from hūs + bonda. Calque of Old Norse húsbóndi. By surface analysis, house + bond.

definition: The content of cognition; the main thing you are thinking about.
example: It was not a good idea.

definition: Indicating the head of a staff.
example: Editor-in-chief.

definition: A relative by marriage.
example: The house got a complete going-over before the arrival of the in-laws.
etymology: Back-formation from -in-law.

definition: Have as a part, be made up out of.
example: The list includes the names of many famous writers.
etymology: From Middle English includen, borrowed from Latin inclūdere (“to shut in, enclose, insert”), from in- (“in”) + claudere (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”). Doublet of enclose.

definition: Enclosed in the same envelope or package.
example: The included check.

definition: A quantity that is added.
example: An increase of about 30% in hits on the website.
etymology: From Middle English encresen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman encreistre, from Latin increscere (“to increase”), from in (“in, on”) + crescō (“grow”). The noun is from Middle English encres, from the verb.

definition: The people or companies engaged in a particular kind of commercial enterprise.
example: Each industry has its own trade publications.

definition: Relating to or being on the side closer to the center or within a defined space.
example: He reached into his inside jacket pocket.
etymology: From Middle English ynneside; equivalent to in- + side.

definition: In place of, or as an alternative to.
example: Felix became a herpetologist instead.
etymology: From in + stead, from Middle English ine (“in”) + stede (“stead”). Related to German statt.

definition: A sense of concern with and curiosity about someone or something.
example: An interest in music.
etymology: From Middle English interest, from Old French interesse and interest (French intérêt), from Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse.

definition: Connected by participation or association or use.
example: We accomplished nothing, simply because of the large number of people involved.
etymology: From involve + -ed.

definition: A land mass (smaller than a continent) that is surrounded by water.
etymology: The insertion of ⟨s⟩—a 16th century spelling modification—is due to a change in spelling to the unrelated term isle, which previously lacked s (cf. Middle English ile, yle).

definition: An important question that is in dispute and must be settled.
example: The issue could be settled by requiring public education for everyone.

definition: The principal activity in your life that you do to earn money.
etymology: From the phrase jobbe of work (“piece of work”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a variant of Middle English gobbe (“mass, lump”);

definition: A room or building equipped with one or more toilets.
example: In-calls, where the john comes to the prostitute’s residence, are prohibited.
etymology: From the male given name John (q.v.), whose ubiquity led to extensive use of the name in generic contexts.

definition: Become part of; become a member of a group or organization.
example: He joined the Communist Party as a young man.
etymology: From Middle English joinen, joynen, joignen, from Old French joindre, juindre, jungre, from Latin iungō (“join, yoke”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, unite”).

definition: And nothing more.
example: Just a scratch.
etymology: From Middle English juste, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic *jowestos, related to Latin iūs (“law, right”);

definition: Cause to continue in a certain state, position, or activity.
example: The students keep me on my toes.
etymology: From Middle English kepe, kep, from the verb (see above).

definition: (especially of promises or contracts) not violated or disregarded.
example: Promises kept.
etymology: From Middle English kept, kepte, from Old English cēpte; see -t.

definition: The (technical) knowledge and skill required to do something.
example: Marlo has the know-how to fix your computer.
etymology: Deverbal from know how. American English, 1838.

definition: Apprehended with certainty.
example: A known quantity.
etymology: From Middle English knowen, from Old English cnāwen (past participle). Morphologically know + -n.

definition: A systematic means of communicating by the use of sounds or conventional symbols.
example: He taught foreign languages.
etymology: Alteration of languet.

definition: Above average in size or number or quantity or magnitude or extent.
example: A large city.
etymology: From Middle English large, from Old French large, from Latin larga, feminine of largus (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”), of uncertain ultimate origin; see there for more.

definition: Immediately past.
example: Last Thursday.
etymology: From Middle English laste, latst, syncopated variant of latest, both ultimately from Old English latost. Doublet of latest.

definition: Being or occurring at an advanced period of time or after a usual or expected time.
example: Late evening.
etymology: From Middle English late, lat, from Old English læt (“slow; slack, lax, negligent; late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lat, from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, lazy”). By surface analysis, deverbal from let.

definition: Happening at a time subsequent to a reference time.
example: He's going to the store but he'll be back here later.
etymology: * Adverb: From Middle English later, latere, from Old English lator, equivalent to late + -er. * Adjective: From Middle English later, latere, from Old English lætra, equivalent to late + -er.

definition: An advantage held by a competitor in a race.
example: He took the lead at the last turn.
etymology: From Middle English led, leed, from Old English lēad (“lead”), from Proto-West Germanic *laud (“lead”), possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd- (“to flow”).

definition: The introductory section of a story.
example: It was an amusing lead-in to a very serious matter.
etymology: Deverbal from lead in.

definition: Indicating the most important performer or role.
example: The leading man.
etymology: From Middle English leding, ledyng, ledinge, ledunge, equivalent to lead + -ing. Cognate with Dutch leiding (“conduit, leading, guidance, leadership”), German Leitung (“line, conduit, cable”).

definition: An association of sports teams that organizes matches for its members.
example: Seven leagues above the mouth of the river we meet with two other passes, as large as the middle one by which we entered.
etymology: From Middle English liege, ligg, lige (“a pact between governments, an agreement, alliance”), from Middle French ligue, from Italian lega, from the verb legare, from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

definition: Gain knowledge or skills.
example: She learned dancing from her sister.

definition: Go away from a place.
example: At what time does your train leave?
etymology: From Middle English leve, from Old English lēaf (“permission, privilege”), from Proto-Germanic *laubō, *laubą (“permission, privilege, favour, worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love, hold dear”).

definition: Make it possible through a specific action or lack of action for something to happen.
example: After he knocked for hours, I decided to let him come in.
etymology: Derived from Middle English letten (“to hinder, delay”), from Old English lettan (“to hinder, delay”; literally, “to make late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lattjan, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną.

definition: A position on a scale of intensity or amount or quality.
example: A high level of care is required.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English levelen, from the noun.

definition: A characteristic state or mode of living.
example: Social life.
etymology: The sense "biography" is likely a semantic loan from Medieval Latin vīta (“biography; hagiography”).

definition: Has a good chance of being the case or of coming about.
example: These services are likely to be available to us all before long.
etymology: From Middle English likely, likly, lykly, likliche, from Old English ġelīclīċ (“suitable”) and Old Norse líkligr (“likely”) (probably independent formations), equivalent to like + -ly (adjectival suffix).

definition: Small in range or scope.
example: Limited war.

definition: Give or make a list of; name individually; give the names of.
example: List the states west of the Mississippi.
etymology: * Finnish lista (“(informal) list; batten”).

definition: Hear with intention.
example: Listen to the sound of this cello.

definition: Actually being performed at the time of hearing or viewing.
example: A live television program.
etymology: An apheretic form of alive.

definition: Pertaining to living persons.
example: Within living memory.
etymology: From Middle English livynge, libbynge, equivalent to live + -ing. Cognate with Middle Dutch levinge, (whence Dutch leving (“way of life, living”)), Middle Low German lēvinge (“living”).

definition: Belonging to time long gone.
example: Those long-ago dresses that swished along the floor.

definition: Relating to or extending over a relatively long time.
example: The long-run significance of the elections.

definition: A person with a strong desire for something.
example: A longer for money.
etymology: From long (“yearn”) + -er.

definition: Perceive with attention; direct one's gaze towards; look.
example: She looked over the expanse of land.
etymology: From Middle English loken, lokien, from Old English lōcian, from Proto-West Germanic *lōkōn. Further origin unknown, no certain cognates outside Germanic.

definition: The act of directing the eyes toward something and perceiving it visually; look.
example: He gave it a good looking at.
etymology: From Middle English lokynge, from earlier lokinde, lokende, from Old English lōciende, present participle of Old English lōcian (“to look”), equivalent to look + -ing.

definition: A person who has general authority over others.
etymology: From Middle English lord and lorde (attested from the 15th century), from earlier (14th century) lourde and other variants which dropped the intervocalic consonant of earlier lowerd, louerd, loverd, laford, and lhoaverd;

definition: Something that is lost.
example: The car was a total loss.
etymology: Pronunciation spelling of lost, representing African-American Vernacular English.

definition: No longer in your possession or control; unable to be found or recovered.
example: A lost child.
etymology: From Middle English loste, losede (preterite) and Middle English lost, ilost, ilosed (past participle), from Old English losode (preterite) and Old English losod, ġelosod, equivalent to lose + -t.

definition: (often followed by ‘of’) a large number or amount or extent.
example: A lot of money.
etymology: From Middle English lot, from Old English hlot (“portion, choice, decision”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlut, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.

definition: Held dear.
example: His loved companion of many years.
etymology: From Middle English loved, luvd, from Old English lufode, first and third person singular past indicative of lufian; and Middle English loved, iloved, from Old English ġelufod, past participle of lufian;

definition: Less than normal in degree or intensity or amount.
example: Low prices.
etymology: Cognate with Scots laich (“low”), Saterland Frisian läich (“low”), West Frisian leech (“low”), Dutch laag (“low”), German Low German leeg, leeg' (“low;

definition: Short and thick; as e.g. having short legs and heavy musculature.
Move something or somebody to a lower position.
example: Lower a bucket into a well.
etymology: From low + -er (comparative suffix).

definition: Produced by a manufacturing process.
example: Bought some made goods at the local store: rope and nails.
etymology: From Middle English mathe, from Old English maþu, maþa (“maggot, worm, grub”), from Proto-Germanic *maþô (“maggot”), from Proto-Indo-European *mot- (“worm, grub, caterpillar, moth”).

definition: Having been surfaced (e.g. with asphalt).
example: He told me a made-up version of the events, but I demanded the truth.

definition: Most important element.
example: The main doors were of solid glass.
etymology: From Middle English mayn, main, maine, mæin, meyn, from main (noun) (see further at etymology 2); compare Old English mæġen (“strong, main, principal”) (used in combination) and Old Norse megn, megenn (“strong, main”).

definition: Of greater importance or stature or rank.
example: A major artist.
etymology: Noun sense 1 is a shortening of sergeant major, perhaps after Spanish mayor in the same sense.

definition: Engage in.
example: Make love, not war.
etymology: Cognate with Scots mak (“to make”), Yola maak, maake (“to make”), North Frisian maage, maaki, mååge (“to make”), Saterland Frisian moakje (“to make; to repair; to prepare; to preach;

definition: Something contrived to meet an urgent need or emergency.
etymology: Deverbal from make do.

definition: An event that is substituted for a previously cancelled event.
etymology: Deverbal from make up.

definition: The act that results in something coming to be.
example: The making of measurements.
etymology: From Middle English making, from Old English macung (“making”), equivalent to make + -ing. Cognate with dated Dutch making (“making”), Old High German machunga.

definition: An adult person who is male (as opposed to a woman).
example: Every man for himself.
etymology: From Middle English man, from Old English mann m (“human being, person, man”), from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *mon- (“human being, man”).

definition: Not of natural origin; prepared or made artificially.
example: Man-made fibers.
etymology: From man (“human”) + made. First attested in 1615. According to the OED, the pronunciation with primary stress on man, /ˈmænˌmeɪd/, is older.

definition: March in a procession.
etymology: From Middle English marche (“tract of land along a country's border”), from Old French marche (“boundary, frontier”), from Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”).

definition: Attach a tag or label to.
example: To mark a box or bale of merchandise.
etymology: From Middle English mark, merk, merke, from Old English mearc (“mark, sign, line of division; standard; boundary, limit, term, border;

definition: The world of commercial activity where goods and services are bought and sold.
example: Without competition there would be no market.

definition: Joined in matrimony.
example: A married man.
etymology: From Middle English maried, imaried, mariet, past participle of Middle English marien (“to marry”), equivalent to marry + -ed.

definition: The pairing of people or things as for comparison or competition.
example: It was a good match-up but the home team won.

definition: A vaguely specified concern.
example: Several matters to attend to.
etymology: Displaced Middle English andweorc, andwork (“material, matter”), from Old English andweorc (“matter, substance, material”), Old English intinga (“matter, affair, business”).

definition: By chance.
example: A small extra effort now can maybe save you much work later.
etymology: From an ellipsis of Middle English it may be, equivalent to may + be. Compare mayhap.

definition: To have the ability to produce a particular effect or achieve an end.
example: A means of control.
etymology: From mean (“method or course of action used to achieve some result”). Compare French moyens, German Mittel.

definition: Relating to the study or practice of medicine.
example: The medical profession.
etymology: Borrowed from French médical, from Medieval Latin medicālis, from Latin medicus. Replaced Old English lǣċe (“doctor (physician)”), which is cognate with Icelandic læknir (“doctor”).

definition: Come together.
example: I'll probably see you at the meeting.
etymology: From Middle English mete, imete, from Old English ġemǣte (“suitable, having the same measurements”), from the Proto-Germanic *gamētijaz, *mētiz (“reasonable;

definition: A formally arranged gathering.
example: Next year the meeting will be in Chicago.
etymology: From Middle English metynge, metinde, metand, from Old English mētende, *ġemētende, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), equivalent to meet + -ing.

definition: The force of workers available.
example: "Muster up the men in the barracks at 0600," the lieutenant said to his sergeant.
etymology: From Middle English men, from Old English menn (“people”), from Proto-Germanic *manniz, nominative plural of Proto-Germanic *mann- (“person”). Cognate with German Männer (“men”), Danish mænd (“men”), Swedish män (“men”).

definition: Send a message to.
example: She messaged the committee.
etymology: From Middle English message, from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”).

definition: Being neither at the beginning nor at the end in a series.
example: The middle point on a line.
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian Middel (“middle”), West Frisian mul (“middle”), Dutch middel (“means; medicine, cure”), German mittel (“middle”, adjective), Mittel (“means;

definition: Physical strength.
example: He pushed with all his might, but still it would not move.
etymology: From Middle English maught, might, miȝt, myght, from Old English maht, meaht, meht, mieht, miht, mæht (“ability, power; strength; virtue”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz (“ability, power;

definition: Of or relating to the study of the principles of warfare.
example: Military law.
etymology: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (“soldier”) + -āris (whence -ary). Doublet of militaire.

definition: The number that is represented as a one followed by 6 zeros.
Excavation in the earth from which ores and minerals are extracted.
etymology: From Middle English min, myn, from Old English mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.

definition: A person authorized to conduct religious worship.
example: Clergymen are usually called ministers in Protestant churches.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer and Latin ministrō, from minister.

definition: A written account of what transpired at a meeting.
Fail to perceive or to catch with the senses or the mind.
example: I missed that remark.
etymology: From mistress.

definition: Not able to be found.
example: Missing in action.
etymology: By surface analysis, miss + -ing.

definition: A hypothetical description of a complex entity or process.
example: The computer program was based on a model of the circulatory and respiratory systems.
etymology: From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.

definition: Informal terms for a mother.
etymology: Clipping of momma.

definition: A particular point in time.
example: The moment he arrived the party began.

definition: The most common medium of exchange; functions as legal tender.
example: We tried to collect the money he owed us.
etymology: In this sense, displaced native Old English feoh, whence English fee. Doublet of mint, ultimately from the same Latin word but through Germanic and Old English, and of manat, through Russian and Azerbaijani or Turkmen.

definition: One of the twelve divisions of the calendar year.
example: He paid the bill last month.
etymology: Eclipsed non-native Old English calend (“month”), borrowed from Latin calendae.

definition: The time period between dawn and noon.
example: I spent the morning running errands.
etymology: From Middle English morwenynge, from morwen + -ynge. By surface analysis, morn + -ing. See also morrow (Middle English morwe).

definition: Used to form the superlative, greatest in size or degree.
example: The king cobra is the most dangerous snake.
etymology: From Middle English most, moste, from Old English mǣst, māst, from Proto-Germanic *maistaz, *maist.

definition: Change location; move, travel, or proceed, also metaphorically.
example: The soldiers moved towards the city in an attempt to take it before night fell.
etymology: From Middle English moven, moeven, meven, borrowed from Old Northern French mover, moveir and Old French mouver, moveir (“to move”) (compare modern French mouvoir from Old French movoir), from Latin movēre (“move;

definition: Being excited or provoked to the expression of an emotion.
example: Too moved to speak.

definition: In motion.
example: A constantly moving crowd.

definition: To a great degree or extent.
example: She's much better now.
etymology: Note that English much is not related to Spanish mucho, and their resemblance in both form and meaning is purely coincidental, as mucho derives from Latin multus and is not related to the Germanic forms.

definition: A necessary or essential thing.
example: Seat belts are an absolute must.
etymology: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most, both from Latin mustum.

definition: Something which is considered required to see.
etymology: Univerbation of must (auxiliary) + see (verb).

definition: Assign a specified (usually proper) name to.
example: They named their son David.
etymology: From Middle English namen, from Old English namian (“to name, mention”) and ġenamian (“to name, call, appoint”), from Proto-West Germanic *namōn (“to name”). Cognate with West Frisian neame (“to name; to mention”).

definition: Of or relating to or belonging to a nation or country.
example: National hero.
etymology: From Middle French national, corresponding to nation + -al.

definition: In accordance with nature; relating to or concerning nature.
example: A very natural development.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English natural, borrowed from Old French natural, naturel, from Latin nātūrālis, from nātus, the perfect participle of nāscor (“be born”, verb). Displaced native Old English ġecynde.

definition: Not far distant in time or space or degree or circumstances.
example: Near neighbors.
etymology: From Middle English nēre, neere (“kidney, abdomen; (pl.) seat of emotions”), probably from unattested Old English *nēora, *nīora, from Proto-West Germanic *neurō, from Proto-Germanic *neurô;

definition: (of actions or states) slightly short of or not quite accomplished; all but.
example: He nearly fainted.
etymology: From near + -ly. Cognate with Scots nerelie, neirlie (“nearly”). Compare also English nearling, nearlings.

definition: A condition requiring relief.
example: She satisfied his need for affection.
etymology: * Old English nēod (“desire, longing”), from Proto-West Germanic *niudi (“desire, eagerness”), from Proto-Indo-European *new- (“to incline, tend, move, push, nod, wave”).

definition: Necessary for relief or supply.
example: A much-needed rest.
etymology: From need + -ed. The adjective is derived from the verb.

definition: In such a manner as could not be otherwise.
example: We must needs be objective.
etymology: The English word is equivalent to need + -'s (possessive marker) and hence to need + -s (suffix forming adverbs).

definition: Newly made.
example: The aroma of new-made bread.

definition: Information about recent and important events.
example: They awaited news of the outcome.
etymology: From Middle English newes, newys (“new things”), equivalent to new (noun) + -s (plural suffix).

definition: Immediately following in time or order.
example: Next in line.

definition: Pleasant or pleasing or agreeable in nature or appearance.
example: What a nice fellow you are and we all thought you so nasty.
etymology: From Middle English nyce, nice, nys, from Old French nice, niche, nisce (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin nescius (“ignorant, not knowing”);

definition: Not functioning properly or in suitable condition for proceeding.
example: The space launch was no-go.

definition: A nonexistent goal.
example: He lived without a reason progressing toward no-goal.

definition: Of a game (or the pitching) in which a pitcher allows the opponent no hits.
example: A no-hit game.

definition: A guest who fails to notify a hotel or restaurant when canceling a reservation.
example: Out of fifty people who said they would attend, we only had three no-shows.

definition: Certain to end in failure and disappointment.
example: A no-win situation.
etymology: From no + win.

definition: Negation of a word or group of words.
etymology: From non- (prefix)

definition: The cardinal compass point that is at 0 or 360 degrees.
example: Minnesota is in the north of the USA.

definition: Negation of a word or group of words.
example: He does not speak French.
etymology: Cognate with Scots nat, naucht (“not”), Saterland Frisian nit (“not”), West Frisian net (“not”), Dutch niet (“not”), German nicht (“not”). Compare nought, naught and aught. More at no, wight, whit.

definition: In the historical present; at this point in the narration of a series of past events.
example: President Kennedy now calls in the National Guard.
etymology: From Middle English nou, nu, from Old English nū, from Proto-West Germanic *nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”). Doublet of nu ("well?").

definition: The property possessed by a sum or total or indefinite quantity of units or individuals.
example: The number of parameters is small.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English number, nombre, numbre, noumbre, from Anglo-Norman noumbre, Old French nombre, from Latin numerus (“number”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute, to give, to take”).

definition: Not in operation or operational.
example: The oven is off.

definition: Located outside a military base.
example: Off-base housing.

definition: A day when things go poorly.
example: I guess this is one of my off-days.

definition: Without previous consideration.
example: I don't know the figures off-hand.

definition: Inaccurate in pitch.
Not on a regular route of a transportation system.
example: An off-line ticket office.

definition: Taking place or located away from the site.
example: An off-site waste treatment operation.
etymology: From off- + site.

definition: Give something useful or necessary to.
example: The conference center offers a health spa.
etymology: From Middle English offren, offrien. In the religious senses inherited from Old English offrian (“to offer, sacrifice, bring an oblation”); otherwise from Old French ofrir.

definition: Place of business where professional or clerical duties are performed.
example: He rented an office in the new building.
etymology: From Middle English office, from Old French office, from Latin officium (“personal, official, or moral duty; official position; function; ceremony, esp.

definition: Any person in the armed services who holds a position of authority or command.
example: An officer is responsible for the lives of his men.
etymology: From Middle English officer, from Anglo-Norman officer, officier, from Old French officer, Late Latin officiarius (“official”), from Latin officium (“office”) + -ārius (“-er”). By surface analysis, office + -er.

definition: Having official authority or sanction.
example: Official permission.
etymology: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), by surface analysis, office + -ial.

definition: Many times at short intervals.
example: We often met over a cup of coffee.
etymology: From Middle English often, alteration (with final -n added due to analogy with Middle English selden (“seldom”)) of Middle English ofte, oft, from Old English oft (“often”), from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”).

definition: A slippery or viscous liquid or liquefiable substance not miscible with water.
example: Oil is found in countries such as Saudi Arabia and is transported all over the world.
etymology: From Middle English oyle, oile (“olive oil”), borrowed from Old French oile, from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”). Compare Proto-Slavic *lojь.

definition: Being satisfactory or in satisfactory condition.
example: Things are okay.
etymology: A respelling of OK.

definition: Adhering to conservative or reactionary principles.
etymology: From old + line (“stated positions of a political or religious group”). Attested from the 19th century, originally in the United States.

definition: Attractively old-fashioned (but not necessarily authentic).
example: A vaulted roof supporting old-time chimney pots.
etymology: From old + time.

definition: Currently happening.
In tune; accurate in pitch.
On a regular route of a railroad or bus or airline system.
example: On-line industries.

definition: Taking place or located at the site.
example: On-site inspection.
etymology: From on + site.

definition: On one occasion.
example: Once I ran into her.
etymology: From Middle English ones, from Old English ānes, a remodelling (after ān (“one”)) of ǣnes, itself an extension of ǣne (“once”) with the genitive suffix -es. Equivalent to one + -s.

definition: One of two equal parts of a divisible whole.
Designed for or restricted to a single person.
example: A one-man show.

definition: A happening that occurs only once and is not repeated.
example: I'll put together a quick one-off as a sample so we can taste the recipe.
etymology: From one + off. Probably from foundry work, in which molds are expensive and generally made to be reusable. A term long used by artists who are printmakers and sculptors to indicate a unique print or casting.

definition: An early ballroom dance; precursor to the fox-trot.
Belonging to some prior time.
example: He was the one-time president of the club.

definition: Moving or permitting movement in one direction only.
example: One-way streets.
etymology: From one + way. First attested in 1906 in reference to one-way tickets; 1914 in reference to one-way streets; 1940 in reference to one-way mirrors.

definition: Completing its life cycle within a year.
On a regular route of a railroad or bus or airline system.
etymology: 1950, from on + line.

definition: And nothing more.
example: He was only a child.
etymology: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz.

definition: Affording unobstructed entrance and exit; not shut or closed.
example: An open door.
etymology: Adjective from Middle English open, from Old English open (“open”), from Proto-West Germanic *opan, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz (“open”), from Proto-Indo-European *upo (“up from under, over”).

definition: In the open air.
example: An open-air theater.

definition: Preceding all others in time or being as first made or performed.
example: The original inhabitants of the Americas.
etymology: From Middle English original, from Old French original, from Late Latin orīginālis (“primitive, original”), from Latin orīgō (“beginning, source, origin”), equivalent to origin + -al; see origin.

definition: Not the same one or ones already mentioned or implied; quantifier, other.
example: Today isn't any other day.
etymology: French autre, Spanish otro, Portuguese outro, etc., all from Latin alter, are false cognates. A true cognate would be Latin anterior.

definition: Not allowed to continue to bat or run.
example: He was tagged out at second on a close play.

definition: Relating to or being on or near the outer side or limit.
example: An outside margin.
etymology: From out + side.

definition: At or to a point across intervening space etc.
example: Come over and see us some time.
etymology: From Middle English over (“riverbank, seashore, brink”), from Old English ōfer (“riverbank, seashore, brink, edge, margin, border”), from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz.

definition: Marked by the reception of pay.
example: A paid official.
etymology: From pay + -ed.

definition: Paid in advance.
example: Paid-up insurance.

definition: A material made of cellulose pulp derived mainly from wood or rags or certain grasses.
