etymology: From Middle English paper, from Anglo-Norman paper, from Old Catalan paper, borrowed from Latin papȳrus (and given the Catalan suffix -er), from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros).

definition: A large area of land preserved in its natural state as public property.
example: There are laws that protect the wildlife in this park.
etymology: From Middle English park, from Old French parc (“livestock pen”), from Medieval Latin parcus, parricus, from Frankish *parrik (“enclosure, pen, fence”). Cognate with Dutch perk (“enclosure;

definition: Something determined in relation to something that includes it.
example: He wanted to feel a part of something bigger than himself.
etymology: From Middle English part, from Old English part (“part”) and Old French part (“part”);

definition: The local environment.
example: He hasn't been seen around these parts in years.

definition: An organization to gain political power.
example: In 1992 Perot tried to organize a third party at the national level.
etymology: From Middle English party, partye, partie, from Anglo-Norman partie, from Old French partie (“side, part; portion, share;

definition: Give money, usually in exchange for goods or services.
example: Pay the waitress, please.
etymology: From Middle English payen, from Old French paiier (“pay”), from Medieval Latin pācāre (“to settle, satisfy”) from Latin pācāre (“to pacify”).

definition: (plural) any group of human beings (men or women or children) collectively.
example: Old people.
etymology: From Middle English peplen, peuplien, partly from Middle French peupler (from peuple (“people”)) and partly from the noun (etymology 1).

definition: Being complete of its kind and without defect or blemish.
example: A perfect circle.
etymology: From Middle English perfit, from Old French parfit (modern: parfait), from Latin perfectus, perfect passive participle of perficere (“to finish”), from per- (“through, thorough”) + facere (“to do, to make”).

definition: By chance.
example: Perhaps she will call tomorrow.
etymology: From Middle English perhappes, perhappous, variant of earlier perhap (“perhaps, possibly”), equivalent to per- + hap (“chance, coincidence”) + -s, on model of Middle English parchaunce (modern perchance).

definition: An amount of time.
example: A time period of 30 years.

definition: Concerning or affecting a particular person or his or her private life and personality.
example: A personal favor.
etymology: From Middle English personal, personele, from Anglo-Norman personel, personal, personell, Old French personal, personel, from Late Latin persōnālis (“of a person, personly”), equivalent to person + -al.

definition: A program in which the audience participates by telephone.
etymology: Deverbal from phone in.

definition: Select carefully from a group.
example: She finally picked her successor.

definition: A baseball play in which a base runner is caught off base and tagged out.
A separate part of a whole.
example: An important piece of the evidence.
etymology: From Middle English pece, peece, peice, from Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, petia (“broken piece, fragment; parcel of land”), of uncertain origin.

definition: A point located with respect to surface features of some region.
example: This is a nice place for a picnic.
etymology: From Middle English placen, from the noun (see above).

definition: A series of steps to be carried out or goals to be accomplished.
example: They drew up a six-step plan.
etymology: Borrowed from French plan (“flat surface, ground plot, map”), from Latin plānus. Some sources also argue for influence or alteration of French plant, from plantar, from Latin plantāre (“set, fix in place”).

definition: Participate in games or sport.
example: We played hockey all afternoon.

definition: (of games) engaged in.
example: The loosely played game.

definition: A person who participates in or is skilled at some game.
example: He is a player for the Australian team.
etymology: From Middle English pleyere, pleyer, from Old English pleġere (“player, athlete, wrestler”), from Proto-West Germanic *plegārī. Equivalent to play + -er.

definition: The act of playing a musical instrument.
etymology: From Middle English playing; equivalent to play + -ing.

definition: Give pleasure to or be pleasing to.
example: These colors please the senses.
etymology: Short for if you please, an intransitive, ergative form taken from if it please you which is a calque of French s'il vous plaît, which replaced pray.

definition: A geometric element that has position but no extension.
example: A point is defined by its coordinates.
etymology: From Middle English poynt, from Old French point m (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin pūnctum (“a hole punched in;

definition: The force of policemen and officers.
etymology: From Middle French police, from Latin polītīa (“state, government”), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía). Doublet of policy, polis (“police”), and polity.

definition: A plan of action adopted by an individual or social group.
example: It was a policy of retribution.
etymology: From Middle English policie, from Old French policie, pollicie and police, from Late Latin politia (“citizenship; government”), classical Latin polītīa (in Cicero), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “citizenship;

definition: Deserving or inciting pity.
example: Oh, you poor thing.
etymology: Displanced native wantsome, Middle English unlede (“poor”, from Old English unlǣde), Middle English unweli, unwely (“poor, unwealthy”, from Old English un- + weliġ (“well-to-do, prosperous, rich”))

definition: Regarded with great favor, approval, or affection especially by the general public.
example: A popular tourist attraction.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English populer, borrowed from Old French populaire, or borrowed from Latin populāris.

definition: The particular portion of space occupied by something.
example: Chief of Staff is the second-highest position in the army.
etymology: From Middle English posicioun, from Old French posicion, from Latin positiō (“a putting, position”), from positus (“placed, situated”), past participle of pōnō (“to place”); see ponent.

definition: Capable of happening or existing.
example: A breakthrough may be possible next year.
etymology: From Middle English possible, from Old French possible, from Latin possibilis (“possible”), from posse, possum (“to be able”); see power.

definition: Affix in a public place or for public notice.
example: Post a warning.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English post, from Old English post (“pillar, door-post”) and Old French post (“post, upright beam”), both from Latin postis (“door, post, doorpost”).

definition: Possession of controlling influence.
example: The deterrent power of nuclear weapons.
etymology: From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent. Compare French pouvoir. Displaced the native Old English anweald.

definition: A customary way of operation or behavior.
example: It is their practice to give annual raises.
etymology: The spelling practice is attested once in Middle English for both the noun and the verb. The noun began to be assimilated in spelling to nouns in -ice; practise (noun) is now obsolete.

definition: Give an exhibition of to an interested audience.
example: To present an envoy to the king.
etymology: From Middle English present, from Old French present, from Latin praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“to be present”), from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + esse (“to be”).

definition: Exert pressure or force to or upon.
example: He pressed down on the boards.
etymology: From Middle English pressen (“to crowd, thring, press”), from Old French presser (“to press”) (Modern French presser) from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere "to press".

definition: Just preceding something else in time or order.
example: The previous owner.
etymology: From Latin praevius.

definition: Confined to particular persons or groups or providing privacy.
example: A private place.

definition: With considerable certainty; without much doubt.
example: He is probably out of the country.
etymology: From Middle English probably, probabily, equivalent to probable + -ly.

definition: A particular course of action intended to achieve a result.
example: The procedure of obtaining a driver's license.
etymology: From Middle English proces, from Old French procés (“journey”), from Latin prōcessus (“course, progression”), nominalization of prōcēdō (“proceed, advance”).

definition: A series of steps to be carried out or goals to be accomplished.
example: Get with the program.

definition: Communicate vividly.
example: He projected his feelings.
etymology: From Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth, extend; expel”). Compare typologically Russian прики́дывать (prikídyvatʹ), прики́дка (prikídka) (akin to кида́ть (kidátʹ));

definition: Something owned; any tangible or intangible possession that is owned by someone.
example: That hat is my property.

definition: Give something useful or necessary to.
example: We provided the room with an electrical heater.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English providen, from Latin prōvidēre (“to foresee, act with foresight”). Doublet of purvey.

definition: Not private; open to or concerning the people as a whole.
example: The public good.
etymology: The adjective and noun are derived from Late Middle English publik, publike (“(adjective) generally observable, public; relating to the general public or public affairs;

definition: Put into a certain place or abstract location.
example: Put your things here.
etymology: From Middle English putten, pitten, pytten, puten, poten, from Old English putian, *pūtian ("to push, put out";

definition: A crushing remark.
example: When he called you a know-it-all, he meant it as a put-down.
etymology: Deverbal from put down.

definition: A composition that imitates or misrepresents somebody's style, usually in a humorous way.
example: I think this is all a big put-on.

definition: A small gasoline engine (as on motor boat).
Planned secretly.
example: It was a put-up job.
etymology: Deverbal from put up.

definition: (of persons) taken advantage of.
An essential and distinguishing attribute of something or someone.
example: The quality of mercy is not strained.

definition: An instance of questioning.
example: There was a question about my training.
etymology: From Middle English questionen, questyonen, partly from Middle French questionner and partly from the noun.

definition: With speed.
example: He works quickly.
etymology: From Middle English quykly, quikliche, quicliche, cwikliche, cwickliche, from Old English cwiculīċe. By surface analysis, quick + -ly.

definition: To a degree (not used with a negative).
example: Quite tasty.
etymology: A development of quit, influence by Anglo-Norman quite. Doublet of coy, quit, quiet, and quietus. For an analogous semantic development from the same root, compare Armenian շատ (šat).

definition: Medium for communication.
example: Send a message by radio.
etymology: Short for radiotelegraphy.

definition: A magnitude or frequency relative to a time unit.
example: They traveled at a rate of 55 miles per hour.
etymology: From Middle English raten (“to scold, chide”), from Old Norse hrata (“to refuse, reject, slight, find fault with”), from Proto-Germanic *hratōną (“to sway, shake”), from Proto-Indo-European *krad- (“to swing”).

definition: On the contrary.
example: Rather than disappoint the children, he did two quick tricks before he left.
etymology: From Middle English rather, from Old English hraþor, comparative of hraþe (“soon, early, fast”). More at rathe. Cognate with Dutch radder (“faster”), comparative of Dutch rad (“fast;

definition: Start an engine again, for example.
Interpret something that is written or printed.
example: Read the advertisement.
etymology: Cognate with Scots rede, red (“to advise, counsel, decipher, read”), Saterland Frisian räide (“to advise, counsel”), West Frisian riede (“to advise, counsel”), Dutch raden (“to advise; guess”), German raten (“to advise;

definition: The output of a computer in readable form.
The cognitive process of understanding a written linguistic message.
example: His main reading was detective stories.
etymology: From Middle English reding, redyng, redand, from Old English rǣdende, present participle of rǣdan (“to read”), equivalent to read + -ing.

definition: Completely prepared or in condition for immediate action or use or progress.
example: She is ready to resign.

definition: Being or occurring in fact or actuality; having verified existence; not illusory.
example: Real objects.
etymology: From Middle English real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs (“matter, thing”), from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”). Doublet of realis.

definition: In accordance with truth or fact or reality.
example: They don't really listen to us.
etymology: From Middle English really, realy, rialliche, equivalent to real + -ly.

definition: A rational motive for a belief or action.
example: The reason that war was declared.

definition: Conforming to the established language usage of educated native speakers.
example: Received standard English is sometimes called the King's English.

definition: New.
example: Recent graduates.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin recēns (genitive recentis).

definition: In the recent past.
example: He was in Paris recently.
etymology: From recent + -ly.

definition: The extended spatial location of something.
example: The farming regions of France.
etymology: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō. Doublet of regio.

definition: Being connected either logically or causally or by shared characteristics.
example: Painting and the related arts.

definition: Merchandise issued for sale or public showing (especially a record or film).
example: A new release from the London Symphony Orchestra.
etymology: From Middle English relesen, relessen, from Old French relaisser (variant of relascher).

definition: Recall knowledge from memory; have a recollection.
example: I can't remember saying any such thing.
etymology: From re- + member.

definition: A written document describing the findings of some individual or group.
etymology: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.

definition: Made known or told about; especially presented in a formal account.
example: His reported opinion.

definition: Necessary for relief or supply.
example: Required course.

definition: Systematic investigation to establish facts.
example: The research station that houses Wang and his team is outside Lijiang, a city of about 1.2 million people.
etymology: Early Modern French rechercher (“to examine closely”), from Old French recerchier (“to seek, to look for”), by surface analysis, re- + search.

definition: (usually preceded by ‘in’) a detail or point.
example: It differs in that respect.

definition: A result.
example: This situation developed in response to events in Africa.

definition: A phenomenon that follows and is caused by some previous phenomenon.
example: The result of a course of action; the result of a mathematical operation.

definition: Go or come back to place, condition, or activity where one has been before.
example: Return to your native land.
etymology: From Middle English returnen, retornen, from Anglo-Norman returner, from Old French retourner, retorner, from Medieval Latin retornare (“to turn back”), from re- + tornare (“to turn”). By surface analysis, re- + turn.

definition: A new appraisal or evaluation.
Being or located on or directed toward the side of the body to the east when facing north.
example: My right hand.
etymology: From Middle English right, righte, from Old English rihte, rehte (“right; rightly; due; directly; straight”), from Proto-Germanic *rehta, from *rehtaz (“right; straight”).

definition: A source of danger; a possibility of incurring loss or misfortune.
example: There is risk of being brutalized, arrested, imprisoned and tortured, all because I want you to know the truth about this matter.
etymology: Cognate with Spanish riesgo, Portuguese risco

definition: A large natural stream of water (larger than a creek).
example: The river was navigable for 50 miles.
etymology: From rive + -er.

definition: The actions and activities assigned to or required or expected of a person or group.
example: Play its role.

definition: An area within a building enclosed by walls and floor and ceiling.
example: The rooms were very small but they had a nice view.
etymology: The word superficially appears to be an exception to the Great Vowel Shift, which might have produced the pronunciation /ɹaʊm/, but the retention of Middle English /uː/ before /m/ is regular.

definition: A charge of ammunition for a single shot.
example: Hospital rounds.
etymology: From Middle English round, rounde, from Old Northern French roünt, rund, Old French ront, runt, reont ( > French rond), from both Late Latin retundus and the original Latin rotundus.

definition: Worn and broken down by hard use.
example: A run-down neighborhood.
etymology: Deverbal from run down.

definition: An angry dispute.
etymology: Derived from the verb run into. For the meaning "end-phase", it presumably comes a marathon race, where in the final part the runners run into the stadium and complete a lap.

definition: (verse) without a rhetorical pause between lines.
example: Most dictionaries cover most adverbs with only run-on entries.

definition: The time at which a (software or multimedia) program is run.
A substantial increase over a relatively short period of time.
example: Jasprit Bumrah has the most unique run-up in the history of cricket.
etymology: Deverbal from run up.

definition: (of fluids) moving or issuing in a stream.
example: As mountain stream with freely running water.
etymology: By surface analysis, run + -ing.

definition: Free from danger or the risk of harm.
example: A safe trip.
etymology: From Middle English sauf, safe, saf, saaf, from Old French sauf, saulf, salf (“safe”), from Latin salvus (“whole, safe”), from Proto-Italic *salawos, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, every”).

definition: Being the one previously mentioned or spoken of.
example: Said party has denied the charges.
etymology: From Middle English seide (preterite) and seid, iseid (past participle), from Old English sǣde, sæġde (preterite) and ġesæġd (past participle), equivalent to say + -ed.

definition: Income (at invoice values) received for goods and services over some given period of time.
example: He's likable and motivated: perfect for a career in sales.

definition: Same in identity.
example: The same man I saw yesterday.
etymology: From Middle English same, samme, samen, (also ysame, isame), from Old English samen (“together”), from Proto-Germanic *samanai (“together”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one, together”).

definition: Save from ruin, destruction, or harm.
example: She was saved from drowning by a passer-by.
etymology: From Middle English saven, sauven, a borrowing from Old French sauver, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”). Displaced native Old English nerian.

definition: A receptacle for catching waste products for further use.
Having rough edges that can be used for sawing.
Express in words.
example: Please say your name slowly and clearly.
etymology: The adverb and interjection are from the verb.

definition: One chap's arbitrary assertion.
example: I wouldn't buy anything that expensive just on the say-so of a saleman.
etymology: From say + so. Compare says who.

definition: A word or phrase that particular people use in particular situations.
etymology: From say + -ing.

definition: A particular branch of scientific knowledge.
example: The science of genetics.
etymology: From Middle English science, scyence, borrowed from Old French science, escience, from Latin scientia (“knowledge”), from sciēns, the present participle stem of scire (“to know”).

definition: 1/60 of a minute; the basic unit of time adopted under the Systeme International d'Unites.
example: They were discounted because they contained blemishes, nicks or were otherwise factory seconds.
etymology: From Middle French seconder, from Latin secundō (“assist, make favorable”).

definition: A self-contained part of a larger composition (written or musical).
example: He always turns first to the business section.
etymology: From Middle English seccioun, from Old French section, from Latin sectiō (“cutting, cutting off, excision, amputation of diseased parts of the body, etc.”), from sectus, past participle of secāre (“to cut”). More at saw.

definition: Perceive by sight or have the power to perceive by sight.
example: You have to be a good observer to see all the details.
etymology: From Middle English se, see, from Old French see, sié (“seat, throne; town, capital; episcopal see”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”), referring to the bishop's throne or chair (compare seat of power) in the cathedral;

definition: Perception by means of the eyes.
etymology: From see + -ing.

definition: Give a certain impression of being something or having a certain aspect.
example: She seems to be sleeping.
etymology: From Middle English semen (“to seem, befit, be becoming”), from Old Norse sœma (“to conform to, beseem, befit”), from Proto-Germanic *sōmijaną (“to unite, fit”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one; whole”).

definition: Your consciousness of your own identity.
Cause to go somewhere.
example: Every day at two o'clock, he sends his secretary out to buy him a coffee.

definition: An organized expression of goodwill at the start of a trip or new venture.
etymology: Deverbal from send off.

definition: A composition that imitates or misrepresents somebody's style, usually in a humorous way.
etymology: Deverbal from send up.

definition: A general conscious awareness.
example: A sense of security.
etymology: From Middle English sense, from Old French sens, sen, san (“sense, perception, direction”); partly from Latin sēnsus (“sensation, feeling, meaning”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive”);

definition: Caused or enabled to go or be conveyed or transmitted.
etymology: From send + -t. See send.

definition: Similar things placed in order or happening one after another.
example: They were investigating a series of bank robberies.

definition: Concerned with work or important matters rather than play or trivialities.
example: A serious student of history.
etymology: From Middle English seryows, from Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, an extension of Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).

definition: Performance of duties or provision of space and equipment helpful to others.
example: The mayor tried to maintain city services.

definition: Put into a certain place or abstract location.
example: Set the tray down.
etymology: From Middle English set, sette, from Old English set (“seat, place of residence, camp, settlement, entrenchment, stable, pen”), from Proto-West Germanic *set (“seat”), from Proto-Germanic *setą (“seat”).

definition: Structure where a wall or building narrows abruptly.
A brief but vigorous fight.
The cardinal number that is the sum of six and one.
example: He wrote three sevens on the paper.
etymology: PIE word *septḿ̥ From Middle English seven, from Old English seofon (“seven”), from Proto-West Germanic *sebun (“seven”), from Proto-Germanic *sebun (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ (“seven”).

definition: A form of all fours in which a total of seven points is game.
(used with count nouns) of an indefinite number more than 2 or 3 but not many.
example: Several letters came in the mail.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman several, from Medieval Latin sēparālis, from Latin sēpar (“separate”). By surface analysis, sever + -al. Not related to severe or seven.

definition: Assets belonging to or due to or contributed by an individual person or group.
example: He wanted his share in cash.
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian skar, sker (“a share in a communal pasture”), Dutch schare (“share in property”), German Schar (“band, troop, party, company”), Icelandic skor (“department”). Compare shard, shear.

definition: Primarily temporal sense; indicating or being or seeming to be limited in duration.
example: A short life.

definition: The act of firing a projectile.
example: The shot was wide of the mark.
etymology: The past participle of shoot.

definition: Give an exhibition of to an interested audience.
example: She shows her dogs frequently.
etymology: Wider cognates include Ancient Greek κῦδος (kûdos), Latin caveō whence English caution and caveat, Sanskrit कवि (kaví, “seer, prophet, bard”), Proto-Slavic *čuti (whence Russian чу́ять (čújatʹ) and many more).

definition: Someone who deliberately behaves in such a way as to attract attention.
example: Quit being such a show-off, before someone gets hurt.
etymology: Deverbal from show off.

definition: A place within a region identified relative to a center or reference location.
example: They always sat on the right side of the church.
etymology: The LGBTQ slang sense was coined by sex therapist and author Joe Kort in 2010 and popularized in 2013.

definition: Having few parts; not complex or complicated or involved.
example: A simple problem.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”, literally “onefold”) (as opposed to duplex (“double”, literally “twofold”)), from semel (“the same”) + plicō (“to fold”).

definition: And nothing more.
example: It is simply a matter of time.
etymology: From Middle English symply, symplely; equivalent to simple + -ly, with *-lely simplified to -ly by haplology.

definition: Term of address for a man.
etymology: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”).

definition: The piece of land on which something is located (or is to be located).
example: A good site for the school.
etymology: From Middle English site, from Anglo-Norman site, from Latin situs (“position, place, site”), from sinere (“to put, lay, set down, usually let, suffer, permit”). Doublet of sitio and situs.

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of five and one.
example: The fives and sixes will have a snack first, then the older kids.
etymology: PIE word *swéḱs From Middle English six, from Old English six, from Proto-West Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

definition: The physical magnitude of something (how big it is).
example: A wolf is about the size of a large dog.
etymology: From Middle English syse, of unclear origin;

definition: Being neither good nor bad.
example: A so-so golfer.
etymology: From Middle English so so, from Old English swā swā, equivalent to so + so. Compare Dutch zozo (“so-so”), German soso (“so-so”), Norwegian så som så (“so-so”).

definition: Relating to human society and its members.
example: Social institutions.
etymology: From Middle French social, from Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion or companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, fellow, partner, associate, ally”), from sequor (“follow”).

definition: An extended social group having a distinctive cultural and economic organization.
A male human offspring.
example: Their son became a famous judge.
etymology: From Middle English sonen, sunen, from the noun (see above).

definition: In the near future.
example: The doctor will soon be here.

definition: A category of things distinguished by some common characteristic or quality.
example: Good sort, bad sort.
etymology: From Middle English sorten, from Old French sortir (“to allot, sort”), from Latin sortīre (“draw lots, divide, choose”), from sors.

definition: Financially secure and safe.
example: Sound investments.
etymology: * Noun: from Middle English sownde, alteration of soun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sun, soun, Old French son, from accusative of Latin sonus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”).

definition: The place where something begins, where it springs into being.
example: Pittsburgh is the source of the Ohio River.

definition: The cardinal compass point that is at 180 degrees.
example: Germany is south of Denmark.

definition: Express in speech.
etymology: From Middle English speke, speken (“to speak”), from Old English specan (“to speak”).

definition: Depleted of energy, force, or strength.
example: A spent cartridge.

definition: Any distinct time period in a sequence of events.
example: We are in a transitional stage in which many former ideas must be revised or rejected.
etymology: From Middle English stage, from Old French estage (“dwelling, residence; position, situation, condition”), from Old French ester (“to be standing, be located”).

definition: A support or foundation.
etymology: From Middle English stand, stande, stond, stonde, stoonde, probably from Middle Dutch stande, from Old Dutch *standan (“to stand”), from Frankish *standan. Forms with -o- may show influence of stonden (“stand”, verb).

definition: Someone who takes the place of another (as when things get dangerous or difficult).
example: The star had a stand-in for dangerous scenes.
etymology: Deverbal from stand in.

definition: Requiring a standing position.
example: A stand-up bar.
etymology: Deverbal from stand up.

definition: A basis for comparison; a reference point against which other things can be evaluated.
example: The schools comply with federal standards.
etymology: From Middle English standard, from Old French estandart (“gathering place, battle flag”), from Frankish *standahard (literally “stand firm, stand hard”), equivalent to stand + -ard.

definition: Take the first step or steps in carrying out an action.
example: Who will start?
etymology: From Middle English stert, from the verb sterten (“to start, startle”). See below.

definition: (especially of eyes) bulging or protruding as with fear.
example: With eyes starting from their sockets.

definition: The territory occupied by one of the constituent administrative districts of a nation.
example: His state is in the deep south.
etymology: From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”).

definition: Stay the same; remain in a certain state.
example: Stay alone.
etymology: From Middle English stay, from Old French estaye, estaie (“a prop, a stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade ("a prop, stay, help, aid";

definition: Any maneuver made as part of progress toward a goal.
example: The police took steps to reduce crime.

definition: Short underpants for women or children.
etymology: From step + in.

definition: The act of increasing something.
example: A step-up in basis.
etymology: Deverbal from step up.

definition: Not in physical motion.
example: Sit there and stay still!
etymology: From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”).

definition: The event of something ending.
example: It came to a stop at the bottom of the hill.
etymology: From Middle English stoppe, from Old English stoppa (“bucket, pail, a stop”), from Proto-Germanic *stuppô (“vat, vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teub- (“to push, hit; stick, stump”). See stoup.

definition: A mercantile establishment for the retail sale of goods or services.
example: Near-synonyms: storeroom, stockroom, warehouse, magazine (archaic).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English store, borrowed from Anglo-Norman stor, from Latin īnstaurāre, from īnstaurō + -āre.

definition: Successive (without a break).
example: Sick for five straight days.
etymology: From Middle English streight, streght, streiȝt, the past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”), from Old English streċċan (past participle ġestreaht, ġestreht), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”).

definition: Having strength or power greater than average or expected.
example: A strong radio signal.

definition: A learner who is enrolled in an educational institution.
example: She is a student of human interactions.
etymology: From Middle English student, studient, from Old French estudiant, estudiente, from Latin studēns, present participle of studeō (“dedicate oneself to, study”). Equivalent to stud(y) + -ent.

definition: A detailed critical inspection.
example: The study of languages is fascinating.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English studien, from Old French estudier (Modern French étudier), from estudie (noun), borrowed from Latin studium. Displaced Old English cneordlæcan.

definition: How something is done or how it happens.
example: In the characteristic New York style.
etymology: * Spanish estilo (“writing tool, stylus; manner of doing something, style; fashionable skill, grace; part of pistil, style”).

definition: An event that accomplishes its intended purpose.
example: Let's call heads a success and tails a failure.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin successus, from succēdō (“succeed”), from sub- (“next to”) + cēdō (“go, move”).

definition: Of the highest quality.
example: A super party.
etymology: From super- (prefix), from Middle English super-, from Latin super-, from super (“above”). Doublet of over and hyper.

definition: The activity of providing for or maintaining by supplying with money or necessities.
example: His support kept the family together.
etymology: From Middle English supporten, from Old French supporter, from Latin supportō.

definition: Having or feeling no doubt or uncertainty; confident and assured.
example: Was sure (or certain) she had seen it.

definition: A set of data arranged in rows and columns.
example: See table 1.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English table, tabel, tabil, tabul, from Old English tabele, tabul, tablu, tabule, tabula (“board”); also as tæfl, tæfel, an early Germanic borrowing of Latin tabula (“tablet, board, plank, chart”).

definition: Carry out.
example: Take action.
etymology: From Middle English taken (“to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike”), from Old English tacan (“to grasp, touch”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse taka (“to touch, take”).

definition: The act of taking in as by fooling or cheating or swindling someone.
etymology: Deverbal from take in.

definition: Understood in a certain way; made sense of.
example: A word taken literally.
etymology: From Middle English taken, takenn, from Old English tacen, *ġetacen, from Old Norse tekinn, from Proto-Germanic *tēkanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to take; grasp; touch”).

definition: Very attractive; capturing interest.
example: Something inexpressibly taking in his manner.
etymology: By surface analysis, take + -ing.

definition: Exchange thoughts; talk with.
example: We often talk business.
etymology: From Middle English talk, talke (“conversation; discourse”), from the verb (see above).

definition: An exchange of ideas via conversation.
etymology: From Middle English talkynge. By surface analysis, talk + -ing.

definition: Levy a tax on.
example: The State taxes alcohol heavily.
etymology: From Middle English taxen, from Anglo-Norman taxer (“to impose a tax”), from Latin taxāre (“to handle, to censure, to appraise, to compute”).

definition: (of goods or funds) not taxed.
etymology: From tax + -free.

definition: Express in words.
example: Tell me what is bothering you.
etymology: From Arabic تَلّ (tall, “hill, elevation”) or Hebrew תֵּל (tél, “hill”), from Proto-Semitic *tall- (“hill”).

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of nine and one; the base of the decimal system.
example: We divided the chocolates into tens to hand out to Hallowe'en visitors.
etymology: PIE word *déḱm̥ From Middle English ten, tene, from Old English tīen, from Proto-West Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

definition: A word or expression used for some particular thing.
example: He learned many medical terms.
etymology: Doublet of terminus and termon. Old English had termen, from the same source.

definition: Status with respect to the relations between people or groups.
example: On good terms with her in-laws.

definition: Put to the test, as for its quality, or give experimental use to.
example: Test this recipe.
etymology: From Middle English teste, from Old French teste, test and Latin testis (“one who attests, a witness”).

definition: The words of something written.
example: There were more than a thousand words of text.
etymology: From Middle English text, from Old French texte, from Medieval Latin textus, from Latin textus (“style or texture of a work”), perfect passive participle of texō (“to weave”). Cognate to texture.

definition: Express gratitude or show appreciation to.
example: She thanked him for the lift.
etymology: From Middle English thank (“gratitude; expression of gratitude, thanks; attractiveness; commendation, praise; God’s grace; goodwill; merit, reward; mind, thought”), from Old English þanc, þonc (“gratitude;

definition: An acknowledgment of appreciation.
example: After all I’ve done, a simple acknowledgment is the thanks I get?
etymology: From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”). More at thank.

definition: Subsequently or soon afterward (often used as sentence connectors).
example: Then he left.

definition: In or at that place or location.
example: They have lived there for years.
etymology: From Middle English there, ther, thare, thar, thore, from Old English þēr, þǣr, þār (“there; at that place”), from Proto-West Germanic *þār, from Proto-Germanic *þar (“at that place;

definition: A special situation.
example: This thing has got to end.
etymology: The word originally meant "assembly", then came to mean a specific issue discussed at such an assembly, and ultimately came to mean most broadly "an object".

definition: Any movable possession (especially articles of clothing).
example: She packed her things and left.

definition: Judge or regard; look upon; judge.
example: I think he is very smart.
etymology: From Middle English thinken, thynken, thenken (also thinchen, thünchen), from Old English þyncan (“to seem, appear”), from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną (“to seem”).

definition: Endowed with the capacity to reason.
etymology: From Middle English thinking, thynkynge, thenkyng, equivalent to think + -ing.

definition: One of three equal parts of a divisible whole.
example: It contains approximately a third of the minimum daily requirement.
etymology: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English thirde, thridde, from Old English þridda, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô, from Pre-Germanic *tretyós, a remodeling of Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós.

definition: (postpositive) however.
example: It might be unpleasant, though.

definition: The content of cognition; the main thing you are thinking about.
example: The thought never entered my mind.
etymology: From Middle English thought, ithoȝt, from Old English þōht, ġeþōht, from Proto-West Germanic *þą̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz, *gaþanhtą (“thought”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think”).

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of one and one and one.
example: Put all the threes in a separate container.
etymology: From Middle English thre, threo, thrie, thri, from Old English þrī, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Doublet of tres and trey.

definition: Involving or relating to three dimensions or aspects; giving the illusion of depth.
example: Lifelike three-dimensional characters.

definition: From beginning to end.
example: Read this book through.
etymology: From Middle English thrugh, þrouȝ, throgh, from Old English þrūh (“trough, conduit, pipe; box, chest;

definition: An instance or single occasion for some event.
example: This time he succeeded.
etymology: * Alemannic German Zimen, Zīmmän (“time, time of the year, opportune time, opportunity”)

definition: A brief suspension of play.
example: Each team has two time-outs left.
etymology: From time + out.

definition: A more or less definite period of time now or previously present.
example: It was a sign of the times.
etymology: Multiplication sense from the idea that something is repeated or added together a given number of times.

definition: A disorderly outburst or tumult.
example: I was embarrassed that they made such a big to-do out of my birthday.
etymology: From to + do, formed on analogy with ado. Compare affair.

definition: The present time or age.
example: The world of today.
etymology: From Middle English today, to-daie, todæig, from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (“today”, literally “on [the/this] day, [this] day forward”), equivalent to to + day.

definition: In contact with each other or in proximity.
example: The leaves stuck together.

definition: The day after today.
example: What are our tasks for tomorrow?

definition: The present or immediately coming night.
example: Tonight is the night.
etymology: From Middle English tonyght, to niȝt, from Old English tō niht.

definition: To a degree exceeding normal or proper limits.
example: There has been a cutback in federal subsidies. Rates have been increasing too.
etymology: From Middle English to (“also, in addition to”), from Old English tō (“furthermore, also, besides”), adverbial use of preposition tō (“to, into”).

definition: An amount needed to restore something to its former level.
example: I added a $20 top-up on my cellphone's data plan.

definition: Add up in number or quantity.
example: When we totalled the takings, we always got a different figure.
etymology: From Middle English total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus (“all, whole, entire”) + -ālis, the former element of unknown origin.

definition: An urban area with a fixed boundary that is smaller than a city.
example: They drive through town on their way to work.

definition: A line or route along which something travels or moves.
example: The track of an animal.
etymology: From Middle English trak, tracke, from Old French trac (“track of horses, trail, trace”), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic source, either Old Norse traðk ("a track; path; trodden spot";

definition: An item of property that is given in part payment for a new one.
etymology: Deverbal from trade in.

definition: Activity leading to skilled behavior.
Change location; move, travel, or proceed, also metaphorically.
example: We travelled from Rome to Naples by bus.
etymology: From Middle English travail, travell, from Old French travail, travaille, travaillie, traval, travalle, traveaul, traveil, traveille, travel. Doublet of travail.

definition: Tested and proved useful or correct.
etymology: From Middle English tried, tryed, equivalent to try + -ed.

definition: Consistent with fact or reality; not false.
example: The story is true.
etymology: Variant of truce.

definition: A fact that has been verified.
example: At last he knew the truth.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English trouthe, from Old English trēowþ, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiþō, from *triwwiz + *-iþō. By surface analysis, true + -th. Doublet of troth.

definition: Make an effort or attempt.
example: Can you start the car? —I'll try (to).
etymology: From Middle English trye, trie, probably from Old French trié, past participle of Old French trier (“to try”).

definition: Putting clothes on to see whether they fit.
etymology: Deverbal from try on.

definition: Hard to endure.
example: Fell upon trying times.
etymology: From try + -ing.

definition: Something causing excitement or stimulating interest.
example: Pretty eyes have always been a turn-on.
etymology: Deverbal from turn on.

definition: Moved around an axis or center.
Involving two parts or elements.
A ballroom dance in duple meter; marked by sliding steps.
Carry on a romantic relationship with two people at the same time.
example: One cowboy two-timed the other in a poker game.

definition: Supported by both sides.
example: A two-way treaty.
etymology: From two + way. Compare Old English twiweġ (“an intersection, a junction of two roads”).

definition: Having a life cycle lasting two seasons.
A subdivision of a particular kind of thing.
example: What type of sculpture do you prefer?
etymology: From Middle English type (“symbol, figure, emblem”), from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).

definition: An organization of employees formed to bargain with the employer.
example: You have to join the union in order to get a job.
etymology: From Middle English unyoun, from Old French union, from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”). Doublet of unio.

definition: Characterized by unity; being or joined into a single entity.
example: Presented a united front.
etymology: From unite + -ed.

definition: The act of using.
example: He warned against the use of narcotic drugs.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English use, from Old French us, from Latin ūsus (“use, custom, skill, habit”), from past participle stem of ūtor (“use”).

definition: Employed in accomplishing something.
example: The principle of surprise is the most used and misused of all the principles of war.
etymology: From Middle English used, equivalent to use + -ed.

definition: A car that has been previously owned; not a new car.
An act that exploits or victimizes someone (treats them unfairly).
Under normal conditions.
example: Usually she was late.
etymology: From Middle English usualli, equivalent to usual + -ly. Broadly displaced native Old English ġewunelīċe (from which English wontly).

definition: A numerical quantity measured or assigned or computed.
example: The value assigned was 16 milliseconds.
etymology: From Middle English valew, value, from Old French value, feminine past participle of valoir, from Latin valēre (“be strong, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”).

definition: Of many different kinds purposefully arranged but lacking any uniformity.
example: His disguises are many and various.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French varieux, from Latin varius (“manifold, diverse, various, parti-colored, variegated, also changing, changeable, fickle, etc.”). By surface analysis, vary + -ous.

definition: Precisely as stated.
example: The very center of town.
etymology: Distantly cognate with Old English wǣr (“true”). Over time displaced the use of a number of Germanic words or prefixes to convey the sense 'very' such as fele, full-, mæġen, sore, sin-, swīþe, (partially) wel.

definition: The visible part of a television transmission.
etymology: From the root vide of Latin videō (“to see”) + -o, formed in analogy to audio.

definition: A way of regarding situations or topics etc.
example: Consider what follows from the positivist view.
etymology: From Middle English vewe, from Anglo-Norman vewe, from Old French veue f (French vue f), feminine past participle of veoir (“to see”) (French voir). Cognate with Italian vedere, as well as Portuguese and Spanish ver.

definition: Go to see a place, as for entertainment.
example: She decided to visit her grandparents for Christmas.
etymology: From Middle English visiten, from Old French visiter, from Latin vīsitō, frequentative of vīsō (“behold, survey”), from videō (“see”).

definition: The distinctive quality or pitch or condition of a person's speech.
example: A shrill voice sounded behind us.
etymology: From Middle English voysen, voicen, from the noun (see above).

definition: Stay in one place and anticipate or expect something.
example: I had to wait on line for an hour to get the tickets.
etymology: Calque of Japanese 待ち.

definition: Being and remaining ready and available for use.
example: Waiting cars and limousines lined the curb.
etymology: From Middle English waitinge, waytynge, waitende, weytende, waitand, waytand, equivalent to wait + -ing.

definition: Use one's feet to advance; advance by steps.
example: Walk, don't run!
etymology: From Middle English walk, walke, walken, walkyn, wolken (“to roll, toss, or turn; to walk; to move; to be living; to beat or full; to perform”), a conflation of Old English wealcan (“to move around; to revolve; to roll;

definition: Person who walks in without having an appointment.
example: The emergency room was overrun with walk-ins.
etymology: Deverbal from walk in.

definition: Not capable of or especially not involving speech or spoken lines.
Close enough to be walked to.
example: The factory with the big parking lot … is more convenient than the walk-to factory.

definition: An apartment in a building without an elevator.
example: There is a walk-up window at the post office.
etymology: Deverbal from walk up. (northern flicker): Imitative of the bird's call.

definition: Feel or have a desire for; want strongly.
example: I want to go home now.
etymology: From Middle English wanten (“to lack, to need”), from Old Norse vanta (“to lack”), from Proto-Germanic *wanatōną (“to be wanting, lack”), from *wanô (“lack, deficiency”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty”).

definition: Desired or wished for or sought.
example: Couldn't keep her eyes off the wanted toy.
etymology: From want + -ed.

definition: Look attentively.
example: Watch a basketball game.
etymology: From Middle English wacchen, from Old English wæċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *wakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *wakjaną.

definition: The act of observing; taking a patient look.
How something is done or how it happens.
example: A lonely way of life.
etymology: Cognate with North Frisian wai, wäi (“way”), Saterland Frisian Wai (“way”), West Frisian wei (“road;

definition: (informal) strikingly unconventional.
example: Hector is one, way-out guy.

definition: Any period of seven consecutive days.
example: It rained for a week.

definition: In fortunate circumstances financially; moderately rich.
example: His family is well-situated financially.

definition: Strongly and firmly constructed.
example: A well-knit argument.
etymology: From Middle English well sett, wel set, wel sette, equivalent to well + set.

definition: The cardinal compass point that is at 270 degrees.
example: We used to live in the west of the country.

definition: A period of indeterminate length (usually short) marked by some action or condition.
example: He was here for a little while.

definition: A married woman; a man's partner in marriage.
example: The Fisherman and His Wife.
etymology: Yet another suggestion connects Old High German weibōn (“move to and fro”), Old Norse veifa (“swing, throw”), for a motive of "one who is moving busily; housekeeper, maidservant" (cf. German Weibel (“manservant, usher”)).

definition: The capability of conscious choice and decision and intention.
etymology: From Middle English willen, from Old English willian (“to will”), from Proto-West Germanic *willjōn (“to will”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”). Cognate with German Low German willen, German willen.

definition: To hope, to desire or to prefer to have something, or to do something.
example: I wish I could go home now.

definition: In accord with the most fashionable ideas or style.
example: A with-it boutique.

definition: On the inside.
etymology: From Middle English withinne, withinnen, from Old English wiþinnan; equivalent to with + in.

definition: An adult female person (as opposed to a man).
example: The woman kept house while the man hunted.

definition: The basic unit of money in South Korea.
etymology: * Past participle of win, from Old English winnan.

definition: The words that are spoken.
example: I listened to his words very closely.

definition: Exert oneself by doing mental or physical work for a purpose or out of necessity; work.
example: I will work hard to improve my grades.

definition: Actively engaged in paid work.
example: The working population.
etymology: From Middle English werking, werkynge, warkynge, worchinge, from Old English wyrċing (“working”), verbal noun of wyrċan (“to work”), equivalent to work + -ing.

definition: Buildings for carrying on industrial labor.
example: The steel works almost fills the valley.

definition: Everything that exists anywhere.
example: In retrospect, the process of economic globalization has meant the end of the world as we knew it.

definition: (often used ironically) worthy of being treated in a particular way.
example: An idea worth considering.
etymology: From Middle English worth, from Old English weorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *werþ, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz (“worthy, valuable”); from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.

definition: Unfulfilled or frustrated in realizing an ambition.
example: Would-be marines have to get through a rigorous examination.

definition: Produce a literary work.
example: My uncle writes newspaper articles for The Herald.
etymology: From Middle English writen, from Old English wrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey- (“to rip, tear”).

definition: The act of creating written works.
example: Writing was a form of therapy for him.
etymology: From Middle English writing, writyng, wryting, wrytyng, from Old English wrīting (“writing”), equivalent to write + -ing.

definition: Set down in writing in any of various ways.
example: Written evidence.
etymology: Morphologically write + -en.

definition: Not correct; not in conformity with fact or truth.
example: The report in the paper is wrong.

definition: Not only so, but.
etymology: Colloquial form of yea or yes. Compare nah. Analyzable as yes + -h.

definition: A period of time containing 365 (or 366) days.
example: She is 4 years old.

definition: Taking place at the close of a fiscal year.
example: Year-end audit.

definition: A late time of life.
example: He's showing his years.

definition: An affirmative.
example: I was hoping for a yes.
etymology: From Middle English yes, from Old English ġīese (“by all means, of course, yes”), derived from the same root as yea. Compare Faroese júsá (“yes, indeed, certainly”).

definition: A person of unquestioning obedience.
Up to the present time.
example: I have yet to see the results.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English yeten, from Old English ġēotan (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-West Germanic *geutan, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).
